title: What makes an animal an animal
description: Animals are many-celled organisms whose cells lack cell walls; they eat other living or dead things, and most can move at some stage of life. Sponges pass the test.

facts.text: Animals are multicellular eukaryotes, and unlike plants and fungi, their cells have no cell walls.
All animals need a source of food: they are heterotrophs, eating other living or dead organisms rather than making their own food.
Most animals can move, at least during some stage of life.
Sponges, which lack muscle tissue, were long considered plants; only after their small movements were noticed in 1765 did their animal nature slowly come to be recognized.
Sponge larvae can swim, but adult sponges do not move from place to place: they spend their lives attached to a surface.
A sponge feeds by filtering water through its porous body; tiny hairlike flagella create currents that bring in bacteria to eat, along with oxygen.

title: The main groups of animals
description: The animal kingdom includes five familiar groups (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish) and a huge crowd of animals without backbones, from insects and crabs to snails, worms, jellyfish, sea stars and sponges.

facts.text: Vertebrates are grouped as fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
Invertebrates include sea stars, sea urchins, earthworms, sponges, jellyfish, lobsters, crabs, insects, spiders, snails, clams and squid.

title: How many animal species are named
description: About 1.5 million animal species have been described, according to IUCN's 2025 table; about 1 million of them are insects. The figure is a snapshot, not an exact count.

facts.text: The IUCN Red List's 2025 table estimates about 1.55 million described animal species (roughly 1.5 million), including about 1 million insects; IUCN cautions the figures are not always up to date.

title: How many species may exist
description: A 2011 study by Camilo Mora and colleagues used patterns in how species sit inside better-known higher groups to estimate about 8.7 million eukaryote species, about 7.8 million of them animals; most are still undescribed.

facts.text: In 2011, Camilo Mora and colleagues estimated about 8.7 million species of eukaryotes on Earth, give or take 1.3 million, of which about 7.77 million (about 7.8 million) are animals.
Mora and colleagues found a steady numerical relationship between counts of the better-known higher groups in classification and the number of species, and used it to predict species numbers.

By the 2011 Mora estimate, about 86 percent of species on land and 91 percent in the ocean are still undescribed, and describing them all the traditional way could take up to 1,200 years and more than 300,000 taxonomists.

title: Vertebrates have a backbone
description: A vertebrate has a backbone, a column of vertebrae that partly encloses the central nervous system. The five vertebrate groups are fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

facts.text: Vertebrates have a backbone (vertebral column), made of vertebrae, which partly encloses the central nervous system, including the spinal cord.

title: Most animals are invertebrates
description: Invertebrates, animals without a backbone, are about 95 percent of described animal species; many wear a hard outer skeleton instead.

facts.text: In the IUCN Red List's 2025 table, about 76,000 of roughly 1.55 million described animal species are vertebrates: roughly 1 in 20, leaving about 95 percent invertebrates.
An invertebrate is any animal without a backbone; more than 90 percent of all living animal species are invertebrates.
Many invertebrates, including most mollusks, crustaceans and insects, have a hard outer skeleton that protects the body and gives muscles something to attach to.

title: Two-part scientific names
description: Carl Linnaeus gave each species a two-part scientific name, genus then species, replacing long descriptive phrases; the system is used internationally, so one name points to one species. Zoological names start from 1758.

facts.text: Carl Linnaeus replaced long descriptive phrase names with two-part names, the genus followed by the species; he named humans Homo sapiens, and his system is internationally accepted among biologists.

The American robin (Turdus migratorius, about 25 cm long) and the European robin (Erithacus rubecula, about 14 cm long) are different birds; colonists named the American one robin because its breast colour resembled the European robin's.
The 10th edition of Linnaeus's Systema Naturae (1758) is the starting point of zoological nomenclature, as Species Plantarum (1753) is for plant names.

title: Ranks of classification
description: Species sit inside ever-larger groups: today's ranks run domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. Close relatives share a genus, like the big cats of Panthera.

facts.text: Linnaeus sorted living things into ranks including kingdom, class, order, genus and species; biologists added more ranks later.
The main ranks of classification today, from broadest to most specific, are domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species.
Lions, tigers, leopards and jaguars all belong to the genus Panthera: the leopard is Panthera pardus and the tiger Panthera tigris.

title: Endotherms and ectotherms
description: Endotherms (mainly mammals and birds) make most of their body heat inside and hold a steady temperature; ectotherms (fish, amphibians, reptiles, invertebrates) absorb it from their surroundings. "Cold-blooded" is misleading: a lizard can be warmer than some mammals.

facts.text: The terms warm-blooded and cold-blooded are imprecise and misleading: some cold-blooded lizards have higher normal body temperatures than some mammals.
Endothermy and ectothermy describe whether most of an animal's heat is generated by internal processes (endo-, inside) or absorbed from the environment (ecto-, outside).
Birds and mammals keep a relatively constant internal temperature whatever the weather: about 37 °C for mammals and about 40 °C for birds.
Fishes, amphibians, reptiles and invertebrates are cold-blooded (ectotherms): their body temperature varies with their surroundings, though they can control it somewhat by behavior such as basking.
Reptiles absorb heat by basking in the sun or lying on warm surfaces, and they move between sun and shade or change body position to control how much heat they gain or lose.

title: The food cost of making your own heat
description: Keeping a steady inside temperature costs energy: reptiles, with a low metabolic rate, need less food than endotherms of the same size and can go long periods without eating.

facts.text: Because reptiles do not keep a constant internal temperature, they have a low metabolic rate, need less food than warm-blooded animals of similar size, and can survive long periods without eating.

title: Herbivores, carnivores and omnivores
description: Herbivores eat mainly plants, carnivores mostly meat, and omnivores regularly eat both; teeth often reveal which.

facts.text: A herbivore feeds mostly on plants; herbivores range from aphids to elephants, and many herbivorous mammals have wide molars that grind leaves and grasses.
A carnivore eats mostly meat; carnivorous mammals have strong jaws and long, sharp teeth to grab and rip apart prey, and all cats, from house cats to tigers, must eat meat.

An omnivore regularly eats both plants and animals, as bears, raccoons and humans do (bears eat berries, mushrooms and animals such as salmon); a raccoon has sharp front teeth for ripping apart mice and large molars for chewing plants, and omnivores can switch foods if one runs out.

title: A diet label is not a family name
description: The giant panda belongs to the order Carnivora and kept a carnivore-like gut, yet it eats mostly bamboo: diet and classification answer different questions.

facts.text: The giant panda is a mammal in the order Carnivora and the bear family, with a digestive system more like a carnivore's, yet bamboo makes up most of its diet.
A giant panda cannot digest cellulose, the main material of bamboo, so it eats 70 to 100 pounds of bamboo a day and spends up to 16 hours a day eating.

title: Food chains and webs
description: A food chain runs from producers, which make their own food, through primary, secondary and tertiary consumers to apex predators, with decomposers recycling the dead; overlapping chains form a food web.

facts.text: Producers (autotrophs) make their own food and form the first level of every food chain; nearly all do it by photosynthesis, from sunlight, carbon dioxide and water.
Primary consumers (herbivores) eat producers, secondary consumers eat the herbivores, tertiary consumers eat the secondary consumers, and apex predators sit at the top.
Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria complete the food chain, turning dead plants and other organic wastes into nutrient-rich soil.
In one ocean food chain, single-celled phytoplankton feed tiny shrimp called krill, and krill are the main food of the blue whale.
All the interconnected and overlapping food chains in an ecosystem make up a food web.

title: The 10 percent rule
description: On average only about 10 percent of the energy at one food-chain level passes to the next; the rest is lost as waste, heat and uneaten dead, which is why most ecosystems have at most five levels.

facts.text: On average only about 10 percent of the energy at one trophic level passes to the next, so of 1,000 units of energy in producers, about 100 reach primary consumers and about 10 reach secondary consumers.

Energy is lost at each step because some food cannot be digested and is excreted, much escapes as heat during respiration, and some organisms die without being eaten; so most ecosystems support at most five trophic levels.

title: What an ecosystem is
description: An ecosystem is a place where living things and nonliving parts such as rocks, temperature and humidity work together; it can be as small as a tide pool, and every part depends on the others.

facts.text: An ecosystem is a geographic area where plants, animals and other organisms, along with weather and landscape, work together; it has living (biotic) parts and nonliving (abiotic) parts such as rocks, temperature and humidity.
Ecosystems come in many sizes: a tide pool is a complete, tiny ecosystem, and every part of an ecosystem depends on every other part, directly or indirectly.

title: Keystone species
description: A keystone species holds its ecosystem together, like the wedge stone at the top of an arch. Robert Paine showed it by removing sea stars from a Washington shore: mussels took over and variety collapsed.

facts.text: In the 1960s, ecologist Robert Paine pried carnivorous ochre sea stars, which eat mussels, off the rocks of Mukkaw Bay, Washington, with a crowbar and threw them into the sea as an experiment.

Within two years of removing the sea stars, California mussels took over rock that had supported anemones, sponges, barnacles, chitons, limpets and seaweeds, and diversity fell sharply; where the sea stars remained, the varied community persisted.
Paine coined the term keystone species for an organism that helps hold its ecosystem together; a keystone is the wedge-shaped stone at the top of an arch that keeps it from collapsing.

title: The largest animal ever
description: The blue whale, a living mammal, is the largest animal known to have lived: up to about 33 meters and more than 150 metric tons, feeding almost only on tiny krill.

facts.text: According to NOAA, the blue whale, a mammal, is the largest animal known to have lived on Earth.
In the Antarctic, blue whales can reach up to about 110 feet (about 33 meters) long and weigh more than 330,000 pounds (about 150 metric tons).
Blue whales feed almost exclusively on krill, and the biggest may eat up to 6 tons of krill a day.

title: The smallest animal record holders
description: The smallest known vertebrate is the Brazilian flea toad (males about 7.1 mm, 2024 study), just below Paedophryne amauensis (7.7 mm); the smallest known adult insects are male fairyfly wasps, as small as 0.139 mm.

facts.text: A February 2024 study in Zoologica Scripta found male Brazilian flea toads (Brachycephalus pulex) average 7.1 mm long, making them the smallest known vertebrate.
The previous smallest-vertebrate record holder was Paedophryne amauensis, a frog from Papua New Guinea whose males average about 7.7 mm.
Males of the fairyfly wasp Dicopomorpha echmepterygis, described in 1997, are the smallest known adult insects: blind, wingless and as small as 0.139 mm, smaller than a single-celled paramecium.
Derived: a 110-foot (about 33,500 mm) blue whale is more than 200,000 times longer than a 0.139 mm male fairyfly.

title: Sorting animals, and diets that change with age
description: Backbone, heat source and diet sort most animals, but some answers change with age: gray tree frog tadpoles eat algae and debris, while adults eat insects.

facts.text: Gray tree frog tadpoles eat algae and organic debris in the water, while adult gray tree frogs mainly prey on insects and their larvae.

title: What makes a mammal
description: Mammals breathe air, make their own heat, have hair at some point in life and feed their young milk from mammary glands; they also share three middle ear bones. Linnaeus named the class after the milk.

facts.text: Carl Linnaeus coined the name Mammalia in 1758, from the Latin mamma, the milk-producing breast, naming the class after its mammary glands.
All mammals breathe air through lungs, are warm-blooded, have hair at some point during life, and produce milk to nurse their young.
In mammals, a chain of three tiny bones carries sound across the middle ear.
Hair is a typical mammal feature, but in many whales it has disappeared except in the fetal stage, before birth.

title: How many mammal species there are
description: The Mammal Diversity Database (July 2026) lists about 6,800 living mammal species, a tiny share of all described animal species.

facts.text: The American Society of Mammalogists' Mammal Diversity Database (version 2.5, July 2026) lists 6,791 living mammal species, about 6,800.
Derived: about 6,800 living mammal species is less than half of one percent of the roughly 1.55 million described animal species (6,791 / 1,550,000 is about 0.44%).

title: Why big cats roar
description: Lions, tigers, leopards and jaguars (genus Panthera) often roar; smaller cats have a fully hardened hyoid bone that prevents roaring. A lion's roar marks territory and carries up to five miles.

facts.text: The big cats of the genus Panthera, especially the lion, often roar; smaller cats have a fully hardened (ossified) hyoid, a small bone in the neck, that prevents them from roaring.
Both male and female lions mark their territory by roaring, and a lion's roar can be heard up to five miles away.

title: Lions in prides, tigers alone
description: Lions are the most social cats, living in prides of related females with their cubs and resident males, and the lionesses do most of the hunting. Tigers, the largest cats, live alone.

facts.text: Lions are the most social cats: they live in prides of related females with their cubs and one or more resident males, from several to as many as 40 animals, and the females are the primary hunters.
The tiger is the largest member of the cat family, and wild tigers live alone except when mating or raising young.

title: The elephant and its trunk
description: Elephants, in three living species, are the largest land animals. The trunk is a boneless fusion of nose and upper lip with about 150,000 muscle bundles, used to smell, breathe, trumpet, drink and grab.

facts.text: There are three living elephant species (African savanna, African forest and Asian), and elephants are the largest living land animals.
An elephant's trunk is a fusion of the nose and upper lip; it contains no bones and has about 150,000 muscle bundles (fascicles).
Elephants use the trunk for smelling, breathing, trumpeting, drinking and grabbing things.

title: Elephant families and the matriarch's memory
description: African elephants live in female-led herds under a matriarch, usually the oldest female. Families led by older matriarchs are better at telling strangers' calls from familiar ones.

facts.text: African elephants live in female-led herds: a matriarch, usually the biggest and oldest female, leads related females and their young, while adult males tend to roam alone or in loose all-male groups.

In a 2001 study in Kenya's Amboseli National Park, researchers played recorded calls to elephant families; families led by matriarchs aged 55 or more told strangers' calls from familiar ones far better, and produced more calves.

title: Whales and dolphins are mammals
description: Whales, dolphins and porpoises breathe air through blowholes, are warm-blooded, have hair at some stage and nurse their young. Dolphins rest half the brain at a time, and bottlenose calves nurse for about 20 months.

facts.text: Whales, dolphins and porpoises (cetaceans) meet the mammal checklist: they breathe air, are warm-blooded, have hair at some point in life and produce milk for their young.
Whales and dolphins breathe through blowholes, nostrils on top of the head: toothed whales have one blowhole opening and baleen whales have two.
Dolphins sleep with only half of the brain at a time, which scientists think lets them keep coming up to breathe even while asleep.
A bottlenose dolphin is pregnant for about 12 months; the calf nurses for about 20 months and stays with its mother for 3 to 6 years.

title: Toothed whales and baleen whales
description: Cetaceans split into toothed whales, which include dolphins and porpoises, and baleen whales, which strain small prey through keratin plates instead of teeth.

facts.text: Cetaceans split into toothed whales, which include dolphins and porpoises, and baleen whales, which have no teeth but plates of baleen, made of keratin like hair and fingernails, that strain small prey from the water.

title: Bats: one mammal species in five
description: There are more than 1,300 bat species, about one in five of all mammal species.

facts.text: There are more than 1,300 species of bats, and bats make up about one-fifth of all mammal species.

title: The only flying mammals
description: Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight; the wing is a modified hand with skin stretched between long fingers.

facts.text: Bats are the only mammals capable of true, sustained flight.
A bat's wing is a modified hand: flexible skin, larger and thinner than the skin between your fingers, stretched between long finger bones; the name Chiroptera means 'hand wing'.

title: Echolocation
description: Many bats find their way and their food by echolocation: they call, mostly in ultrasound, and listen for the echoes, calling faster as they close in on an insect.

facts.text: In echolocation, bats send out sound waves that bounce off objects and return to their ears; most bat calls are ultrasound, too high-pitched for humans to hear.
When a bat detects an insect it wants to eat, it produces a rapid series of calls to pinpoint the prey's exact location.

title: Marsupials: born early, raised in a pouch
description: Marsupial young are born tiny and embryo-like and finish developing outside the womb, usually in a pouch. A red kangaroo is born after about 33 days at the size of a jellybean.

facts.text: Marsupial young are born in an embryo-like state and continue developing outside the womb, making their own way to the shelter, warmth and milk of the pouch; in some species there is no full pouch and the nipples are exposed.
A red kangaroo is born after a pregnancy of about 33 days, about the size of a jellybean, and climbs straight into its mother's pouch.
A red kangaroo joey leaves the pouch for good at around 235 days old but keeps suckling until about 12 months; red kangaroos are the largest living marsupials, with males about 2 m tall.

title: Where marsupials live
description: Most marsupials live in Australia, New Guinea and nearby islands; the rest live in the Americas, and the Virginia opossum is the only one north of Mexico.

facts.text: Most marsupial species live in Australia, New Guinea and nearby islands; the rest live in the Americas, mainly South and Central America.
The Virginia opossum is the only marsupial found north of Mexico; its young are born after 12 to 13 days, about 14 mm long, and climb into the mother's pouch.

title: Monotremes: mammals that lay eggs
description: The platypus and the echidnas are monotremes, the only mammals that lay eggs. The first platypus skin in Europe was suspected to be a hoax.

facts.text: When a platypus skin first reached Europe, some naturalists suspected a hoax, perhaps a duck's bill attached to a mole's body; George Shaw scientifically described the animal in 1799.
Monotremes, the platypus and the four living species of echidna, are the only mammals that lay eggs; they still feed their young milk.
The platypus lives only in Australia; the short-beaked echidna lives in Australia, and the long-beaked echidna is from New Guinea.

title: How egg-laying mammals raise their young
description: Platypus eggs hatch in about ten days and the young lick milk from fur-covered patches, since monotremes have no nipples. A young echidna suckles in the pouch until its spines grow.

facts.text: A platypus mother usually lays one or two eggs and keeps them warm between her body and her tail; they hatch in about ten days.
Monotremes have no nipples: when platypus young hatch, the mother secretes milk from two fur-covered milk patches on her belly, and the young suckle it there.

A short-beaked echidna lays one egg at a time; it hatches after about 10 days, and the young suckles in the mother's pouch for two or three months until its spines make it too prickly, when she moves it to a burrow.

title: What makes a primate
description: Primates have forward-facing eyes with overlapping views, flat nails instead of claws, and large brains for their body size.

facts.text: Primates' eyes face forward so their fields of view overlap; primates have flat nails where other mammals have claws or hooves; and for its body weight, the primate brain is larger than other land mammals'.

title: Apes and monkeys
description: Apes are tailless primates, unlike most monkeys. The great apes are gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and orangutans, and humans are in the same family.

facts.text: Apes are tailless primates, while most monkeys have tails; the great apes are gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and orangutans, and humans belong to the same family, Hominidae.

title: Our closest living relatives
description: Chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living relatives, with about 1.2 percent DNA difference. Humans did not evolve from any living primate: we share ancestors.

facts.text: Chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living relatives: their DNA differs from ours by about 1.2 percent, gorillas' by about 1.6 percent and rhesus monkeys' by about 7 percent.
Humans did not evolve from any primate living today; humans and chimpanzees descend from a shared ancestor species that lived millions of years ago.

title: Dogs came from ancient wolves
description: Dogs came from an ancient gray wolf population not well represented by wolves alive today, at least 15,000 years ago; where and how many times is still debated.

facts.text: A 2014 genome study found that dogs and today's wolves share a common ancestor that lived 9,000 to 34,000 years ago; dogs came from an ancient wolf population not well represented by any wolves alive now.
Dogs originated from the gray wolf during the Ice Age, at least 15,000 years ago; where this happened, and whether it happened once or more than once, is still unknown.
A 2022 study of 72 ancient wolf genomes found dogs closer to ancient wolves from eastern Eurasia: an eastern source contributed to all dogs, and a second, more westerly source to some.

title: The Oberkassel puppy
description: About 14,000 years ago a sick puppy buried with two people at Oberkassel, Germany, survived for weeks only with human care: the earliest known evidence of dogs treated as pets.

facts.text: About 14,000 years ago at Oberkassel, Germany, a puppy was buried with a man and a woman; it caught canine distemper at about 19 weeks and likely lived to about 28 weeks only thanks to intensive human care.
Researchers call the Oberkassel puppy the earliest known evidence of dogs being regarded and treated as pets.

title: Egg, pouch or placenta
description: Mammals start life three ways: monotremes lay eggs, marsupials finish growing in a pouch, and placental mammals, everyone else, grow in the womb fed by a placenta. Elephants carry their young up to about 22 months.

facts.text: In placental mammals a placenta passes nutrients and wastes between the mother's blood and the unborn baby's, so the young reach an advanced stage before birth; placentals are all living mammals except marsupials and monotremes.
Elephants are pregnant for up to about 22 months, longer than any other mammal.

title: What makes a bird a bird
description: Feathers set birds apart from all other animals; not every bird flies. Birds have toothless beaks (jaws in a horny sheath) and lay hard-shelled eggs.

facts.text: Feathers are the major characteristic that distinguishes birds from all other animals.
Not all birds can fly: flightless birds such as ostriches have given up flight.
A bird's bill is its upper and lower jaws covered by a horny sheath; many beaked animals, including all birds and turtles, lack teeth.
Birds reproduce by laying hard-shelled eggs.

title: A light skeleton for flight
description: In the largest flying birds part of the bone is replaced by air; hollow wing bones are braced by internal struts. A frigatebird's skeleton weighs less than its feathers.

facts.text: In the largest flying birds, part of the bone is replaced by air cavities, making a pneumatic skeleton.
To keep the walls of a bird's hollow wing bones from buckling, the bones have internal strut-like reinforcements.
The skeleton of a frigatebird with a seven-foot wingspan weighs less than the feathers covering it.

title: How a bird's wing lifts and pulls
description: A wing makes lift by turning the airflow, which pushes back the opposite way (Newton's third law). A bird's wing is also its propeller: the inner wing mostly lifts, the wing tip mostly pulls it forward.

facts.text: Lift occurs when a moving flow of air is turned by a solid object such as a wing: the flow turns one way and lift acts the opposite way (Newton's third law), and both upper and lower surfaces help turn the flow.
A bird's wing acts as both wing and propeller: the inner part of the wing supplies most of the supporting surface, and the wing tip most of the propelling force.

title: Flight muscles and the keel
description: Flying birds anchor their flight muscles on the keel, a ridge on the breastbone. The large pectoralis pulls the wing down; the smaller supracoracoideus lifts it.

facts.text: Flying birds have a keel, a ridge on the sternum (breastbone) that is a main site of attachment for the flight muscles.
Birds power flight mainly with large pectoralis muscles that pull the wings down; the smaller supracoracoideus, about one-fifth the size of the pectoralis, raises the wing on the upstroke.

title: Bird nests, from nothing to woven
description: Nests range from no real structure (falcons, owls, many seabirds and shorebirds) to woven weaver nests, built of twigs, leaves, mud, feathers or spiderwebs, from about 2 cm to more than 2 m across.

facts.text: Bird nests range from no real structure at all (in falcons, owls and many seabirds and shorebirds) to the elaborate flask-shaped nests that weavers weave from grass.
Bird nests are made of twigs, leaves, mud, feathers or even spiderwebs, and some swifts use saliva as cement.
Bird nests range from about 2 cm across in small hummingbirds to more than 2 m in large eagles, and in weight from a few grams to more than a ton.

title: Incubation and hatching
description: A sitting bird warms its eggs through a bare, blood-rich brood patch, near 38 °C, and turns them. The chick breaks out with an egg tooth that it soon loses.

facts.text: Toward the end of egg-laying, incubating birds lose the feathers from a patch of belly skin, the brood patch, which grows extra blood vessels bringing hot blood close to the surface; if both parents incubate, both may grow one.
The ideal incubation temperature for most birds is around 38 °C; the sitting bird raises or lowers its body to adjust it and turns the eggs as they develop.

A chick breaks its shell with the egg tooth, a hard tip on its bill whose role William Yarrell discovered in 1826; in most birds it falls off a few days after hatching, while in perching birds it is absorbed into the bill.

title: Birds of prey and how they kill
description: All birds of prey have hook-tipped beaks and talons. Eagles and hawks kill mainly with their feet, squeezing prey; falcons kill with a bite, using the tomial tooth on the beak.

facts.text: All birds of prey have hook-tipped beaks and sharp curved claws called talons.
The daytime birds of prey (hawks, eagles, vultures and falcons) are also called raptors; the owls are the nocturnal birds of prey.
Eagles, hawks and their relatives have weaker bites than falcons and no beak 'teeth'; they kill by constricting prey with their feet, with two unusually massive talons for grip.
Falcons catch prey with their feet but often kill it with a bite to the neck, using the tomial tooth, a sharp notched ridge on the upper beak.

title: The peregrine falcon's dive
description: In 1999 a trained peregrine named Frightful was clocked at 242 mph diving from nearly three miles up; Audubon says wild peregrines may possibly reach 200 mph.

facts.text: In 1999 a trained peregrine falcon named Frightful, flown by falconer and skydiver Ken Franklin, was clocked at 242 mph (about 389 km/h) diving from nearly three miles up, measured by a small chip on her tail feathers.
Some falcon experts criticized Franklin's dives as artificial, because wild peregrines do not usually start dives from such heights.
Audubon's field guide says that in power-diving from great heights to strike prey, the peregrine falcon may possibly reach 200 mph.

title: Owls hunt by ear
description: Barn owls can strike prey in total darkness by sound alone (Payne and Drury, 1958). Lopsided ears let them find a sound's height as well as direction, and the facial disc funnels sound to the ears.

facts.text: In 1958 Payne and Drury showed a barn owl could locate mice by sound in total darkness: when a mouse towed a crumpled wad of paper, the owl struck the paper, ruling out sight and smell.
A barn owl's ears are asymmetrical, one slightly above the other; the difference in sound level between the ears tells the owl a sound's height, helping it pinpoint prey in three dimensions.
Barn owls have the greatest ability of any animal tested to locate prey by ear.
All owls have a facial disc of short feathers around the face; the barn owl's heart-shaped disc works like a satellite dish, funneling sound towards the ears.

title: Owls' silent flight
description: Serrated leading edges, a velvety surface and soft trailing fringes on owl feathers muffle flight, so prey can't hear the owl and the owl can keep hearing its prey.

facts.text: Owl wing feathers have comb-like serrations on the leading edge, a velvety texture and a soft fringe on the trailing edge, which together damp the sound of flight.
Silent flight may help owls in two ways: prey can't hear them coming, and the owl can keep hearing and tracking its prey.

title: Penguins are built to swim
description: Penguins' wings became flippers, and their limb bones are dense with almost no air spaces, cutting buoyancy for diving. Emperor penguins dive to about 550 m, deeper than any other bird.

facts.text: Penguins are flightless birds of the Southern Hemisphere whose wings evolved into flippers that power them underwater.
Penguin limb bones are denser than those of nearly all other birds and almost entirely lack air spaces; dense bone is usually interpreted as reducing buoyancy and saving energy in diving.
Emperor penguins, the deepest-diving birds on Earth, can dive to about 550 m (1,800 feet).

title: How penguins stay warm
description: Dense waterproof feathers, a thick fat layer and a countercurrent heat exchanger in the legs and feet keep penguins warm; emperor males fast for 9 weeks through the Antarctic winter on their fat.

facts.text: Penguins are insulated by a dense layer of short, stiff, waterproof feathers that trap air and by a thick layer of fat.
A countercurrent heat-exchange system in penguins' legs and feet minimizes the heat they lose to ice and cold water.
Penguins huddle in large groups to share body heat and shelter from harsh weather.
Emperor penguins breed in the coldest, darkest months of the Antarctic winter, and the male incubates the egg for 9 weeks without eating, relying on a thick fat reserve.

title: The hummingbird's engine
description: A ruby-throated hummingbird's heart runs from about 225 beats a minute at rest to more than 1,200 in flight. Hummingbirds are the only vertebrates that can hover for long, beating their wings about 70 times a second.

facts.text: A ruby-throated hummingbird's heart beats about 225 times a minute at rest and more than 1,200 times a minute in flight.
An active hummingbird's heart pumps at about 1,200 beats per minute, while a human athlete's heart reaches only about 150 during exercise.
Hummingbirds are the only vertebrates capable of sustained hovering, and they can fly backward and upside down.
A ruby-throated hummingbird's wings beat about 70 times a second in direct flight and more than 200 times a second while diving.

title: Hummingbird energy and torpor
description: Weighing 2 to 20 grams, with poor insulation and huge metabolic demands, hummingbirds can drop into torpor on cold nights; a black metaltail cooled to 3.3 °C in a 2020 study.

facts.text: Hummingbirds weigh 2 to 20 grams; their feathers offer poor insulation and they have incredibly high metabolic demands.

Hummingbirds can go into torpor any night when temperature and food demand it: a deep, sleep-like state with metabolism slowed to a minimum and a very low body temperature, used when they cannot keep their normal warmth.

In a study published in 2020, a black metaltail hummingbird in the Peruvian Andes cooled to 3.26 °C (about 3.3 °C) in torpor, the lowest body temperature recorded for any bird or non-hibernating mammal.

title: New Caledonian crows make tools
description: Wild New Caledonian crows make standardized hook tools from twigs and pandanus leaves (Hunt, 1996). In a 2002 Oxford study, Betty bent a straight wire into a hook to lift food from a tube.

facts.text: In 1996 Gavin Hunt reported in Nature that wild New Caledonian crows make and use two kinds of hook tool, hooked twigs and stepped-cut tools from barbed pandanus leaves, with standardized, distinct tool types.
New Caledonian crows use their tools to forage for invertebrates in dead wood.

In a 2002 Oxford study, a captive New Caledonian crow named Betty, left with a straight wire after another crow, Abel, took the hooked one, bent the wire into a hook and lifted a small bucket of food from a tube; it was only the crows' fifth experience with wire.

title: Alex the African grey parrot
description: Irene Pepperberg's African grey parrot Alex learned to identify 50 objects, 7 colors, 5 shapes and quantities up to 6.

facts.text: Alex, an African grey parrot studied by Irene Pepperberg for about 30 years, learned to identify 50 objects, 7 colors, 5 shapes and quantities up to 6, plus a zero-like concept; he died in 2007 at age 31.

title: Small brains, packed with neurons
description: A 2016 study found parrot and songbird brains hold about twice as many neurons as primate brains of the same mass; large-brained parrots and corvids match or beat primates with bigger brains in forebrain neurons.

facts.text: A 2016 PNAS study of 28 bird species found parrot and songbird brains hold on average about twice as many neurons as primate brains of the same mass.
Large-brained parrots and corvids (the crow family) have as many forebrain neurons as primates with much larger brains, or more.

title: Record-breaking bird migrations
description: In 2022 a juvenile bar-tailed godwit flew about 13,560 km nonstop from Alaska to Tasmania in 11 days. Tracked Arctic terns fly about 70,900 km a year (2010 study), with one Farne Islands tern estimated at 96,000 km (2016).

facts.text: In October 2022 a juvenile bar-tailed godwit tagged B6 flew nonstop about 13,560 km (8,425 miles) from Alaska to Tasmania, Australia, in 11 days, tracked by a 5-gram solar-powered satellite tag: the longest documented nonstop flight by any animal.

In a 2010 PNAS study, 11 Arctic terns from Greenland and Iceland carrying 1.4-gram geolocators flew an average of 70,900 km a year between the Arctic and the Southern Ocean, with a North Atlantic stopover: the longest round-trip animal migration recorded electronically.
In 2016 Newcastle University reported that one geolocator-tagged Arctic tern from England's Farne Islands made an estimated 96,000 km round trip to the Weddell Sea, Antarctica.
Because Arctic terns can live more than 30 years, the 2010 study estimated a tern's lifetime migrations may exceed 2.4 million km, about three return trips to the Moon.

title: Fuel and navigation for migration
description: Migrants fuel long flights with stored fat (some double their weight; B6 fattened up in Alaska) and find their way using the sun, the stars and Earth's magnetic field.

facts.text: Before its record flight, the godwit B6 fattened up on Alaska's Kuskokwim Delta, then flew without stopping for food, water or rest.
Some migratory birds double their body weight before migrating by gorging on berries, insects or mollusks.
Migrating birds can sense which direction they are flying from the position of the sun, the stars and Earth's magnetic field.

title: The ostrich: a bird that gave up flying
description: The ostrich, the largest living bird, cannot fly: like other ratites it has no keel on its breastbone to anchor flight muscles. It runs instead, on two-toed feet, and lays the world's largest egg.

facts.text: The ostrich, a flightless bird of open country in Africa, is the largest living bird: an adult male may stand 2.75 m tall and weigh more than 150 kg.
A frightened ostrich can run at about 70 km/h (Britannica gives 72.5 km/h, 45 mph), and it is the only two-toed bird, its main toe developed almost as a hoof.
Ratites, including the ostrich and emu, have a smooth, raftlike breastbone that lacks a keel to anchor flight muscles, so they cannot fly.
The ostrich lays the largest egg of any living bird, averaging about 15 cm long.

title: Reptile scales keep water in
description: Most reptiles wear a continuous coat of scales made mostly of keratin; with waxy lipids, this skin cuts water loss and helped reptiles live on land.

facts.text: Most reptiles have a continuous covering of scales, and keratin is the main component of reptile scales.
Keratin is the tough, fibrous structural protein of hair, nails, horns, hoofs, feathers and the outer layers of skin.
Reptiles' scaly skin, containing keratin and waxy lipids, reduces water loss; it was one of the key adaptations that let reptiles live on land.

title: The amniotic egg
description: A reptile embryo grows inside the amnion, a fluid-filled sac, within a leathery or hard shell that holds water in, so reptiles can lay eggs on dry land; most amphibians still lay soft, jelly-like eggs in water.

facts.text: In a reptile egg the embryo is enclosed in the amnion, a membranous, fluid-filled sac that gives it its own internal watery environment.
Reptile eggs have a leathery or hard, calcium-based shell that holds in water and nutrients for the embryo; some reptiles instead give birth to live young.
The amniotic egg freed early vertebrates from needing water to reproduce, so reptiles can lay eggs on dry land; most amphibians still lay soft, jelly-like eggs in water.

title: The living reptile groups
description: Today's reptiles are turtles, the tuatara, lizards and snakes, and crocodilians: more than 12,500 species, most of them ectotherms.

facts.text: The major groups of living reptiles are turtles, the tuatara, lizards and snakes, and crocodilians, together more than 12,500 species; most are ectotherms.

title: How snakes move without legs
description: Limbless snakes move in four main ways: serpentine loops that push against rocks and twigs, rectilinear creeping on belly scales, concertina and sidewinding.

facts.text: Snakes differ from other reptiles in being limbless, with a greatly elongated body and tail, and they lack movable eyelids and external ear openings.
Snakes have four main ways of moving: serpentine (lateral undulation), concertina, rectilinear and sidewinding, which is used on sand.
In serpentine movement a snake's body forms S-shaped loops, and each loop pushes against whatever resistance it finds, such as rocks, twigs or pebbles.
Heavy-bodied snakes such as boas often creep in a straight line (rectilinear movement), lifting, anchoring and pushing with their belly scales like a caterpillar.

title: Snakes smell with their tongues
description: A snake's flicking tongue carries scent particles to the Jacobson's organ in the roof of its mouth; the two tips of the fork give it directional, stereo smell.

facts.text: When a snake flicks its tongue it captures scent particles from the air or ground and delivers them to the Jacobson's organ on the roof of its mouth, which detects smells.
Each tip of a snake's forked tongue samples a different spot, giving the snake a stereo sense of smell that tells it which side a scent is stronger on.

title: How snakes swallow big prey
description: A snake's two lower jaw halves are not joined at the chin, so they spread wide and move independently, and stretchy skin widens the gape; most snakes swallow prey whole.

facts.text: Unlike a human lower jawbone, the two halves of a snake's lower jaw are not joined at the chin, so they can spread wide and move independently.
Most snakes swallow prey whole, and they can swallow prey much larger than their heads by walking their mouth over it, and stretchy skin widens the gape.
A wild Burmese python in Everglades National Park was found with an adult white-tailed deer it had swallowed.

title: Venom versus poison
description: Venom is injected through a wound by a fang, stinger or spine; poison harms when it is eaten or absorbed through the skin.

facts.text: Venom must be injected, by a bite or sting, to cause harm, whereas poisons are harmful when ingested or absorbed through the skin.
Venomous animals deliver toxins by wounding, often with a fang, stinger or spine, while poisonous animals such as pufferfishes deliver them passively when touched or eaten.

title: What venom does
description: Venom is a mixture of toxic enzymes and proteins; neurotoxins attack the nervous system, up to paralysis that stops breathing, and hemotoxins attack blood and blood vessels.

facts.text: Venoms are made in specialized glands and are mixtures of toxic enzymes and other proteins; neurotoxins attack the nervous system, and hemotoxins attack blood and blood vessels, causing bleeding or disrupting clotting.
Snake venom can cause paralysis that may prevent breathing, and bleeding disorders that can lead to fatal hemorrhage.

title: How antivenom is made
description: Since Albert Calmette's cobra antivenom in the 1890s, antivenom has been made by giving horses (or sheep) small doses of venom and collecting the antibodies their immune systems make.

facts.text: French scientist Albert Calmette created the first snake antivenom, against cobra venom, in the 1890s, and in 1895 began producing it by inoculating horses.

Most antivenoms are made in horses, some in sheep: a small amount of venom is injected, the animal's immune system makes antibodies, and they are harvested from its blood; the method has changed little in over 120 years.
WHO estimates about 81,000 to 138,000 people (81,410 to 137,880) die from snakebites each year, and says antivenom is the most effective treatment and most deaths are preventable.

title: A turtle's shell is its skeleton
description: The carapace is built from the turtle's backbone and ribs fused to bony plates; with the plastron it forms a rigid box the turtle can neither leave nor shed.

facts.text: A turtle's shell has a carapace on top and a plastron below, joined along each side into a rigid skeletal box; the turtle cannot leave it, and it is not shed.
A turtle's carapace is built from its backbone (trunk vertebrae) and ribs, fused to bony plates that form in the skin.

title: Every tortoise is a turtle
description: 'Turtle' covers the whole shelled order of more than 350 species; tortoises are the land-only branch, while other turtles live in fresh water or the sea.

facts.text: All tortoises are turtles, but not all turtles are tortoises: tortoises live only on land, while other turtles live in fresh water or the sea.
There are more than 350 species of turtles (Britannica counts about 356), living on every continent except Antarctica.

title: Nest temperature sets a sea turtle's sex
description: Sea turtle eggs below about 27.7 °C hatch male and above about 31 °C female; warming beaches in the northern Great Barrier Reef now produce almost only females.

facts.text: Sea turtle eggs that incubate below 27.7 °C hatch as males, and above 31 °C as females; temperatures in between give a mix.
A NOAA-led study published in 2018 found that 99.1 percent of juvenile green turtles from the warmer northern Great Barrier Reef nesting beaches were female.

title: Crocodilians, built to lurk
description: Crocodiles, alligators, caimans and gharials form the crocodilians; eyes, ears and nostrils on top of the head let them watch and breathe while hidden underwater.

facts.text: The crocodilians include alligators, crocodiles, gharials and caimans.
A crocodilian's eyes, ears and nostrils sit on top of its head, so they stay above water while the rest of its body is submerged.

title: Telling crocodiles from alligators
description: Crocodiles have narrow, V-shaped snouts and show some lower teeth with the mouth closed; alligators have broad, U-shaped snouts with lower teeth tucked inside, the big fourth tooth hidden in a socket.

facts.text: Crocodiles have a narrow, V-shaped snout and show some lower teeth when the mouth is closed; alligators have a broad, U-shaped snout, with lower teeth fitting inside the upper ones.
An alligator's large fourth tooth in the lower jaw fits into a socket in the upper jaw and is hidden when the mouth is closed; in crocodiles it is not.

title: Salt glands and saltwater crocodiles
description: Alligators lack salt glands and stay mostly in fresh water; crocodiles have salt glands in their tongues, which lets the saltwater crocodile, the largest living crocodilian, travel far out to sea.

facts.text: Alligators are usually found in fresh water and can tolerate salt water only for brief periods, because they do not have salt glands.
Crocodiles, including the saltwater (estuarine) crocodile, have salt glands in their tongues that get rid of excess salt.
The saltwater crocodile is the largest living crocodilian, growing up to 23 feet (about 7 meters), and is sometimes seen far out at sea.

title: How chameleons change colour
description: A 2015 University of Geneva study showed panther chameleons shift colour by tuning a lattice of guanine nanocrystals in skin cells called iridophores: packed close they reflect blue, loosened they reflect yellows and reds.

facts.text: Chameleons are a group of mostly tree-dwelling Old World lizards best known for their ability to change colour.
Many vertebrates change colour by spreading out or gathering pigment-containing granules inside skin cells, and chameleons use pigment too.
In 2015, a University of Geneva team showed that panther chameleons change colour by actively tuning a lattice of guanine nanocrystals in skin cells called iridophores.
When a panther chameleon is calm its nanocrystals sit close together and reflect blue; when excited it loosens the lattice, reflecting yellows and reds.

title: Why chameleons change colour
description: Chameleons' dramatic colour changes are mainly signals to other chameleons and responses to temperature and light, not attempts to match the background; darkening helps an ectotherm warm up.

facts.text: It is a popular misconception that chameleons change colour to match their background; their colour changes respond to light, temperature and emotional states such as fright, victory or defeat.
Panther chameleons make their fastest, most complex colour changes in social encounters such as male contests and courtship, within a minute or two.
Chameleons are ectotherms, and darker colours absorb more light, so a chameleon can darken to warm up faster when basking.
A deeper layer of larger crystals in a panther chameleon's skin reflects much of the sun's infrared, which may protect it from overheating.

title: Amphibians: a double life
description: 'Amphibian' loosely means 'dual life'; many start life in water and change shape as they grow; most lay soft, shell-less eggs in water or damp places; the class has three branches: frogs, salamanders and caecilians.

facts.text: The word amphibian loosely translates from Greek as 'dual life', a reference to the metamorphosis many frogs and salamanders go through.
All living amphibians fall into three groups: frogs, salamanders and the legless caecilians.
Most amphibians lay soft, jelly-covered eggs without a shell, in water or damp places.

title: Amphibian skin drinks and breathes
description: Amphibians have moist, permeable skin kept wet by mucus glands; they take in most of their water through it and use it as one of their breathing surfaces.

facts.text: Amphibians have moist, permeable skin kept wet by mucus glands; most of their water is taken in across the skin rather than by drinking, and the skin is one of their three breathing surfaces.

title: Chytrid and the amphibian crisis
description: The chytrid fungus attacks amphibian skin and upsets the body's salt balance until the heart stops; it has driven declines in at least 501 species, and IUCN's 2023 assessment found 41% of amphibian species threatened.

facts.text: IUCN's second Global Amphibian Assessment, published in 2023, found 41 percent of assessed amphibian species threatened with extinction, making amphibians the most threatened class of vertebrates.
Disease from the chytrid fungus was the leading cause of worsening extinction risk for amphibians from 1980 to 2004; since 2004, climate change has led.
The chytrid fungus infects amphibian skin and disrupts the salts it moves into the body, until the heart stops.
A 2019 study led by Ben Scheele linked chytrid fungus disease to declines in at least 501 amphibian species over the past half-century, including 90 presumed extinctions.

title: From tadpole to frog
description: A tadpole has gills and a finned tail and no legs; during metamorphosis hind legs sprout first, then lungs and front legs, the tail is absorbed, the mouth turns froglike and the gills disappear.

facts.text: Tadpoles usually have gills and long, finned tails, lack limbs, and are often plant-eaters.
In a tadpole's metamorphosis the hind legs sprout first; then lungs develop and the front legs appear, the tail gradually shrinks, and the gills disappear just before it becomes a frog.
During metamorphosis a tadpole's lungs develop, its limbs appear, its tail is absorbed and its mouth becomes froglike; the change takes from two months to three years.

title: Thyroid hormone drives metamorphosis
description: In 1912 Friedrich Gudernatsch found that feeding tadpoles horse thyroid, and no other organ, sped up metamorphosis; removing a tadpole's thyroid stops it. Thyroid hormone directs the change.

facts.text: In 1912, Friedrich Gudernatsch fed tadpoles several horse organs and found that only the thyroid gland sped up their metamorphosis.
Removing a tadpole's thyroid gland stops metamorphosis: the changes are controlled by thyroid hormone and fail to happen without it.

title: Naming the dinosaurs
description: After William Buckland described Megalosaurus in 1824, Richard Owen proposed the group Dinosauria in 1842, from Greek deinos ('terrible' or 'fearfully great') and sauros ('reptile' or 'lizard'); dinosaurs were a diverse group of reptiles.

facts.text: In 1824, William Buckland described Megalosaurus from fossils consisting mainly of a lower jawbone with a few teeth.
Richard Owen proposed the name Dinosauria in 1842, based on remains of three giant extinct animals.
The name dinosaur comes from the Greek deinos ('terrible' or 'fearfully great') and sauros ('reptile' or 'lizard').
Dinosaurs were a diverse group of reptiles.

title: What made a dinosaur a dinosaur
description: Dinosaurs held their legs straight under the body like pillars instead of sprawling like lizards, and had a hole through the hip socket; pterosaurs and sea reptiles such as plesiosaurs were reptiles on separate branches.

facts.text: Dinosaurs held their limbs under the body in columnar fashion, like elephants, rather than sprawled out to the sides like modern lizards.
Dinosaurs have a hole in their hip socket, while pterosaurs' hip sockets are a bony depression.
Flying pterosaurs and marine reptiles such as plesiosaurs and ichthyosaurs were reptiles that evolved separately from dinosaurs, so they were not dinosaurs.

title: Dinosaur eggs and nests
description: In 1978 a Maiasaura nesting site near Choteau, Montana, turned up nests of eggs, eggshells and babies; the babies could not yet walk but had worn teeth, so parents likely fed them. Dinosaurs laid eggs like the reptiles they were.

facts.text: In 1978 a Maiasaura nesting site was found near Choteau, Montana, with nests holding clutches of eggs, many broken eggshells and baby dinosaurs.
Paleontologists Jack Horner and Bob Makela named the dinosaur Maiasaura, 'good mother lizard', because babies too young to walk had worn teeth, suggesting parents fed them.

title: Salamander or lizard?
description: Salamanders look like lizards but are amphibians: smooth, moist skin, no claws, no ear openings and eggs in jelly, versus a lizard's dry scales, claws and leathery-shelled eggs. Many salamanders even breathe without lungs.

facts.text: Salamanders have smooth, moist skin and eggs encased in clear jelly; lizards have dry, scaly skin and eggs in a leathery shell.
Most lizards have claws on their toes and ear openings; salamanders have neither.

Great Smoky Mountains National Park has more salamander species than anywhere else on Earth, more than 30, and most of them are lungless, breathing through their skin and the linings of their mouths and throats.

title: How fish breathe with gills
description: Fish breathe through gills: water flows over blood-rich gill filaments, oxygen dissolved in the water passes into the blood, and carbon dioxide passes out.

facts.text: Fish breathe through gills, which extract oxygen dissolved in water: as water flows over the gill filaments, which are rich in blood vessels, oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out into the water.

title: Fins and scales
description: Paired pectoral fins steady and steer a fish, working with its back and tail fins; the scales of bony fishes are thin overlapping plates of bone that keep growing all its life.

facts.text: The pectoral fins, a fish's paired side fins, are crucial for stabilization and steering, working with the dorsal (back) and caudal (tail) fins to keep balance and control movement.
Unlike the scales of cartilaginous fishes, the scales of bony fishes, when present, are thin overlapping plates of bone that grow throughout the fish's life.

title: The warm-blooded opah
description: Most fish species are cold-blooded, but the opah is warm-blooded, keeping warm with a heat-exchange system in its gills.

facts.text: Most fish species are cold-blooded, but one, the opah (Lampris guttatus), is warm-blooded; its warmth comes from a heat exchange system in its gills.

title: Sharks: boneless and older than trees
description: Sharks are cartilaginous fishes with no bones, only lightweight, flexible cartilage like that in your ear; they have been around for about 400 million years, longer than trees (about 350 million).

facts.text: Sharks are cartilaginous fishes: they have no bones, and their skeleton is cartilage, which is lightweight and flexible, like the cartilage in a human ear.
Sharks have been around for about 400 million years, while the earliest trees, such as the extinct Archaeopteris, lived around 350 million years ago.

title: How sharks sense their world
description: NOAA counts eight shark senses. Sharks smell blood from far off, and a lateral line of pores from snout to tail lets sensory cells detect pressure changes in the water.

facts.text: NOAA lists eight shark senses: hearing, smell, lateral line, pit organs, vision, ampullae of Lorenzini, touch and taste.
Sharks have an acute sense of smell and can smell blood in the water from a long way away.
A shark's lateral line is a row of small pores running from snout to tail; as water flows through them, sensory cells detect pressure changes.

title: Shark bites are rare
description: The International Shark Attack File confirmed 65 unprovoked shark bites worldwide in 2025, in line with recent years and, in its words, extremely low.

facts.text: The International Shark Attack File confirmed 65 unprovoked shark bites worldwide in 2025, in line with the 2020-2024 average of 61 a year, and calls the total extremely low.

title: The dark, hungry deep sea
description: Below about 1,000 meters no sunlight reaches the ocean. Darkness, cold, pressure and distance from the sunlit plankton at the base of the food chain limit deep-sea life.

facts.text: Light may be detected as far as 1,000 meters down in the ocean, but rarely significantly beyond 200 meters; below 1,000 meters sunlight does not reach and the water is dark.
In the deep midnight zone, darkness, high pressure, cold and the great distance from the base of the food chain (plankton, which need sunlight) limit how much life can live there.

title: Deep-sea animals that make light
description: Most deep-sea animals can glow: a 2017 MBARI study found three quarters of animals from the surface to 4,000 meters in Monterey Bay make light. Female anglerfish use a glowing lure lit by bacteria.

facts.text: A 2017 MBARI study by Severine Martini and Steve Haddock found that three quarters of the animals seen in Monterey Bay waters, from the surface to 4,000 meters deep, can make their own light.

Adult female anglerfishes of most species carry a lure, the esca, on a "fishing rod"; it glows with bioluminescent bacteria living inside it, and prey drawn in meet large, sharp, backward-pointing teeth.

title: An octopus thinks with its arms
description: The common octopus has about 500 million neurons, as many as a dog, and about two thirds are in its arms, so arms can work on problems while the brain does other things. Octopuses open wired-shut clams, run mazes and remember solutions.

facts.text: The common octopus has about 500 million neurons, about as many as a dog, and about two thirds of them are in its arms, which lets arms work on problems while the central brain handles other tasks.
Octopuses can figure out how to open a clamshell that has been wired shut, navigate mazes, solve problems and remember the solutions.

title: Three hearts and blue blood
description: An octopus has three hearts: two pump blood past the gills and one pumps it to the body (and stops when the octopus swims). Its blood is blue because its oxygen carrier, hemocyanin, uses copper instead of iron.

facts.text: An octopus has three hearts: two move blood past its gills, and the third sends oxygen-rich blood to the organs and muscles; that third heart stops beating when the octopus swims.
Octopus blood is blue because its oxygen-carrying protein, hemocyanin, contains copper rather than the iron of the hemoglobin in human blood.

title: A body with no brain or heart
description: A jellyfish is about 95 percent water, with no brain, blood or heart; a nerve net senses its world, and one opening serves as mouth and anus.

facts.text: Only about 5 percent of a jellyfish's body is solid matter; the rest, about 95 percent, is water. Jellyfish lack brains, blood and hearts, and sense their surroundings with a simple nerve net.
A jellyfish's simple digestive cavity acts as both stomach and intestine, with one opening serving as both mouth and anus.

title: How jellyfish sting
description: Jellyfish sting with nematocysts: capsules holding coiled harpoons that fire in about 700 nanoseconds, hard enough to pierce a crustacean shell.

facts.text: Jellyfish sting with nematocysts, capsules with tiny harpoons coiled inside; when triggered, hundreds fire in jabs lasting about 700 nanoseconds, with force enough to pierce a crustacean's shell.

title: Coral is a colony of animals
description: A coral is hundreds to thousands of tiny animals called polyps, each building a limestone skeleton. Corals are animals because they catch food instead of making it, using stinging nematocysts like their jellyfish relatives.

facts.text: Corals are animals, not plants, because they do not make their own food; because they attach permanently to the ocean floor, many people think they are plants.
Most structures called coral are made up of hundreds to thousands of tiny animals called polyps; each soft-bodied polyp, most no thicker than a nickel, secretes a hard outer skeleton of limestone.
Coral polyps capture food with tentacles armed with stinging cells called nematocysts, the same kind of stinging cells used by jellyfish, which are relatives of corals.

title: Coral bleaching
description: Most corals house algae (zooxanthellae) that are their main food and color. Stressed corals, above all by warmer water, expel the algae and turn white; they can recover if the stress eases, or die if it lasts.

facts.text: Most corals contain microscopic algae called zooxanthellae in their tissues; sheltered by the coral, the algae photosynthesize and are the coral's primary food source, and they give the coral its color.
When corals are stressed by changes in temperature, light or nutrients, they expel their algae and turn completely white; NOAA names rising ocean temperature from climate change as the leading cause.
A bleached coral is not dead: if the stress is not severe it can recover, but if the algae loss is prolonged and the stress continues, the coral eventually dies.

title: A salmon's round trip
description: Sockeye salmon hatch in fresh water, go to sea to grow, then swim upstream to spawn where they were born, turning red. All die within weeks, and their bodies feed the river and the next generation.

facts.text: Most sockeye salmon hatch in freshwater streams, rivers or lakes, spend 1 to 3 years in fresh water, then migrate to the ocean to feed and grow, typically returning after 2 to 3 years at sea.
Adult sockeye migrate many miles upstream to spawn, usually in the stream or lake of their birth; their bodies turn bright red, and all sockeye die within a few weeks of spawning.
Bears and eagles feed on sockeye in fresh water, and after salmon spawn and die, their carcasses supply energy and nutrients to the river, improving the growth and survival of newly hatched salmon.

title: How salmon find their home stream
description: Before heading to sea, young salmon imprint on the smell of their home stream, and adults follow those odor memories back; they also imprint on Earth's magnetic field where they enter the sea.

facts.text: Before migrating to sea, juvenile salmon learn (imprint on) the particular odors of their home stream, and maturing adults use those odor memories to guide their homing migration.
Salmon also imprint on the Earth's magnetic field at the place where they first enter the sea.

title: Life between the tides
description: The intertidal zone lies between high and low tide; its middle floods and drains twice a day. Residents survive low tide by closing up in shells or moving to water that stays; hermit crabs reuse empty shells.

facts.text: The intertidal zone is where the ocean meets the land between high and low tides; in its middle zone the tides ebb and flow twice a day, and sea stars and anemones live there.
Intertidal animals get through low tide by closing up in their shells to stay moist and ward off predators, or by moving to a zone that stays underwater; hermit crabs reuse empty shells.

title: Sea stars: tube feet and an outside stomach
description: Sea stars are not fish (no gills, scales or fins). They move and grip on tube feet, regrow lost arms, and eat mussels by pulling the shell open and pushing their stomach inside.

facts.text: Sea stars are not fish: they have no gills, scales or fins. They move on tiny tube feet on their undersides, which also help them hold prey, and they can regrow a lost arm.
A sea star opens a clam or mussel by pulling on the shell with its suction feet, then inserts its stomach into the shell and digests the prey.

title: Plankton: the ocean's drifters
description: Plankton are living things carried by tides and currents because they cannot swim against them. Phytoplankton are plant drifters; zooplankton are animal drifters such as krill, young fish and jellyfish, which rise to the surface at night to feed.

facts.text: Plankton, from the Greek for drifter, are organisms carried by tides and currents that cannot swim against them; they are usually microscopic but include larger species such as jellyfish.
Plankton divide into phytoplankton (plants) and zooplankton (animals); zooplankton include krill, the young of fish and larger invertebrates, and jellyfish, and most eat phytoplankton.
Zooplankton generally stay in deeper water by day to avoid predators and rise to the surface at night to feed on phytoplankton, a journey considered the largest migration on Earth.

title: Phytoplankton make oxygen
description: Phytoplankton photosynthesize like plants, so they live near the sunlit surface. Roughly half of Earth's oxygen production comes from the ocean, mostly from plankton.

facts.text: Like plants on land, phytoplankton photosynthesize, taking in carbon dioxide and producing oxygen; because they need the sun's energy, they live near the water's surface.
Scientists estimate that roughly half of the oxygen production on Earth comes from the ocean, mostly from photosynthesizing plankton; marine life uses about the same amount.

title: Fish: nearly half of all vertebrates
description: Of about 76,000 described vertebrate species in IUCN's 2025 table, about 37,000 are fish: nearly half of the backbone family.

facts.text: IUCN's 2025 table lists about 37,000 described fish species (37,109) among about 76,000 described vertebrates (76,289): nearly half.

title: The insect body plan
description: An insect’s body has three parts: a head with a pair of antennae, a thorax carrying six legs and usually wings in adults, and an abdomen; its skeleton is on the outside.

facts.text: An insect’s body has three regions: the head, with mouthparts, eyes and one pair of antennae; the thorax, with three pairs of legs and, in adults, usually one or two pairs of wings; and the abdomen, with the digestive and reproductive organs.
Insects have external skeletons (exoskeletons).

title: How many insects there are
description: About 1 million insect species have been described, and the Smithsonian estimates some 10 quintillion individual insects are alive at any one time. Both are estimates.

facts.text: The Smithsonian estimates about 10 quintillion (10,000,000,000,000,000,000, a 1 followed by 19 zeros) individual insects are alive at any one time; the largest insect orders include beetles, flies, ants and moths.

title: How an ant colony works
description: An ant colony’s queen lays the eggs; the workers are sterile females who build, defend and feed; males only mate and then die. Some ants lay pheromone scent trails for nestmates to follow.

facts.text: Worker ants are sterile females, rarely winged, that construct, repair and defend the nest and feed the young and adult ants of the colony, including the queen.
The primary function of an ant queen is reproduction (laying eggs), and a queen may live for many years.
The sole function of a male ant is to mate with an unfertilized female reproductive; after mating, the male dies.
Some ants leave scent trails made of chemicals called pheromones, which other ants follow to the food source.

title: Leafcutter ants farm fungus
description: Leafcutter ants do not eat the leaves they cut: they feed them to a fungus they grow, and the fungus feeds the colony. Ants farmed fungus tens of millions of years before people farmed.

facts.text: Leafcutter ants do not eat the leaves they cut: they use them to nourish a fungus they grow as food for the colony, and that fungus is found only with the ants, not in the wild.
Ants were farming fungus for tens of millions of years (about 60 million, by one Smithsonian account) before humans began agriculture about 12,000 years ago.

title: How honeybees make honey and wax
description: Honeybee workers (all females) turn nectar into honey with enzymes, fan it with their wings to evaporate water, and seal it in comb built from wax made by their own glands. Honey is about 18 percent water.

facts.text: In honeybees, enzymes break the complex sugars of nectar into simpler ones, turning it into honey; the bees beat their wings to promote evaporation, then seal the cells with wax.
Nectar ripens into honey as most of its sucrose is converted to simpler sugars and excess moisture is removed; honey contains about 18 percent water and is stored in honeycomb made of beeswax.
A worker honeybee has four pairs of wax glands on the underside of her abdomen; workers build comb from this wax as two layers of six-sided cells.
Honeybee workers are females that do not reach sexual maturity; males (drones) are present only part of the year.

title: How bees pollinate flowers
description: Pollination moves pollen from a flower’s anther to a stigma. Pollen catches in a bee’s branched hairs as she feeds and rubs off on the next flower; honeybees also carry pollen home in leg baskets.

facts.text: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from a flower’s male anther to the female stigma; flowers rely on vectors such as wind, water, insects, birds and bats to move pollen.
Most bees have a dense coat of branched hairs that help collect pollen, and while feeding at a flower a bee may deposit pollen on its stigma.
Honeybee workers have pollen baskets (corbiculae) on their hind legs for collecting pollen.
Pollinators get food, energy-rich nectar and/or protein-rich pollen, from the flowers they visit, and in return the flowers get pollen carried from one flower to another.

title: Complete metamorphosis
description: A butterfly passes through four stages, egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa (chrysalis) and adult, a process called complete metamorphosis.

facts.text: The monarch butterfly has four life stages, egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa (chrysalis) and adult, called complete metamorphosis; eggs hatch about four days after being laid, and larvae grow from under 1 cm to about 5 cm.

title: Rebuilding a caterpillar into a butterfly
description: Inside the chrysalis, a caterpillar dissolves most of its tissues into caterpillar soup, while imaginal discs, grown before it hatched, survive and build the adult’s wings, legs and eyes.

facts.text: Inside the chrysalis a caterpillar releases enzymes that dissolve most of its tissues into caterpillar soup, though some muscles and parts of the nervous system are kept.

While still in its egg, a caterpillar grows imaginal discs, one for each adult body part such as eyes, wings and legs; they survive in the chrysalis and use the soup to divide fast (a fruit fly wing disc grows from about 50 to more than 50,000 cells).

title: Spiders are arachnids, not insects
description: Spiders are arachnids: two body parts (cephalothorax and abdomen), eight legs and no antennae. Nearly all are predators, mostly of insects.

facts.text: Spiders are arachnids with a body in two parts, the cephalothorax and the abdomen, rather than three, eight legs rather than six, and no antennae.
All spiders except the nearly herbivorous Bagheera kiplingi are predators, feeding mostly on other arthropods, especially insects; not all spiders build webs.

title: How spiders make silk and webs
description: Spider silk starts as a liquid protein in abdominal glands and hardens as it leaves through the spinnerets. Many night-hunting orb weavers eat their webs at dawn, recycling the protein, and rebuild each night.

facts.text: Spider silk starts as a liquid protein made in glands in the abdomen and hardens as it is drawn out through the spinnerets, silk-producing organs usually on the underside of the abdomen.

Many nocturnal orb weavers take down and eat their webs toward dawn and rebuild them each night; eating the silk returns its protein to the silk glands for new silk, and an orb web takes about 30 to 45 minutes to make.

title: Snails, slugs and the mollusks
description: Snails and slugs are gastropods, the largest group of mollusks (soft-bodied invertebrates, usually in a shell made by the mantle). They move on one muscular foot over mucus; slugs are snails whose shells shrank or vanished in evolution.

facts.text: Slugs are snails whose shells have been reduced to an internal fragment or completely lost in the course of evolution.
Mollusks are soft-bodied invertebrates, usually wholly or partly enclosed in a calcium carbonate shell secreted by the mantle, a layer covering the body.
Mollusks include snails, slugs and limpets (gastropods); clams, mussels and oysters (bivalves); and squids, cuttlefishes and octopuses (cephalopods).
Gastropods, the snails and slugs, are the largest group in the phylum Mollusca.
Gastropods move on a foot, a muscular organ driven by waves of contraction, and land snails and slugs glide on a track of mucus.

title: The radula
description: Snails and slugs eat with a jaw and a radula, a flexible band of thousands of microscopic teeth that rasps food like sandpaper.

facts.text: Snails and slugs eat with a jaw and a radula, a flexible band of thousands of microscopic teeth; the jaw cuts off larger pieces such as a leaf, and the radula rasps them.
A snail’s radula is a membrane covered with rows of tiny teeth made of chitin, so it is coarse like sandpaper.

title: Earthworm bodies breathe through skin
description: Earthworms have no lungs and breathe through moist skin; their bodies are chains of ringlike segments.

facts.text: Earthworms lack lungs and breathe through their skin, which must stay moist; they need surroundings with at least 40 percent moisture.
An earthworm’s body is divided into ringlike segments, as many as 150 in Lumbricus terrestris.
Earthworms live in soil and usually go unnoticed, except after a heavy rain, when they come to the surface.

title: How earthworms help the soil
description: Earthworms eat decaying plants and soil, open burrows for air, water and roots, and leave casts richer than the surrounding soil. Darwin’s 1881 book estimated they move more than ten tons of earth per acre each year.

facts.text: Earthworms eat decaying plants and other organisms, swallowing large amounts of soil as they do; they aerate the soil, promote drainage and draw organic material into their burrows.
Deep earthworm burrows create passages for air, water and roots, and worm casts are richer than the surrounding soil, with nutrients in forms more available to plants.

Charles Darwin’s book on earthworms, The Formation of Vegetable Mould through the Action of Worms, came out in October 1881, sold 6,000 copies within a year and at first sold far faster than On the Origin of Species.

Darwin estimated that in many parts of England more than ten tons of dry earth per acre pass through worms’ bodies each year and are brought to the surface, and wrote that long before people existed the land was regularly plowed by earthworms.

title: Crustaceans and their armor
description: Crabs, lobsters, shrimps and wood lice are crustaceans, with two pairs of antenna-like feelers and an outer skeleton stiffened with calcium carbonate.

facts.text: Crabs, lobsters, shrimps and wood lice (pill bugs) are crustaceans; crustaceans have two pairs of antenna-like appendages (antennules and antennae) in front of the mouth.
In crustaceans, extra rigidity comes from an exoskeleton impregnated with varying amounts of calcium carbonate.

title: Molting to grow
description: A rigid outer skeleton cannot grow, so crabs and lobsters molt: they climb out, stretch a soft new skeleton with water or air, and hide while it hardens. Lobsters often eat the old shell to regain calcium.

facts.text: A rigid exoskeleton limits growth, so arthropods such as crabs and lobsters periodically shed it (molting); the new exoskeleton is soft and flexible, is stretched by taking in water or air, and then hardens.
American lobsters molt about 20 to 25 times over 5 to 8 years between hatching and being able to reproduce.

A newly molted soft-shelled crab is extremely vulnerable to damage and predators and stays hidden or buried for a few days while its new shell expands and starts to harden; the shell keeps hardening for two to three months.
Lobsters eat voraciously after molting, often devouring their own recently shed shells, which replenishes lost calcium and helps harden the new shell.

title: Only female mosquitoes bite
description: Only female mosquitoes bite, because they need a blood meal to produce eggs; both sexes drink nectar and fruit juices. Anopheles mosquitoes develop in water from egg to larva to pupa to adult.

facts.text: Mosquitoes (family Culicidae) are insects, about 3,500 species, some important to public health because the females suck blood.
Only female mosquitoes bite people and animals, because they need a blood meal to produce eggs; both females and males feed on flower nectar and fruit juices.
Female Anopheles mosquitoes lay eggs directly on water; the larvae and the pupae live in the water, and pupae do not eat; egg to adult takes 10 to 14 days, and adult females bite.

title: Mosquitoes carry deadly germs
description: Mosquitoes pick up germs from infected people and animals and spread them by biting; malaria parasites travel this way. WHO estimated 610,000 malaria deaths in 2024, and the CDC calls the mosquito the world’s deadliest animal.

facts.text: The CDC calls the mosquito the world’s deadliest animal; mosquitoes spread diseases including malaria, dengue, West Nile, Zika, chikungunya and lymphatic filariasis.
Mosquitoes become infected with germs, such as viruses and parasites, when they bite infected people and animals, and spread them through later bites.
Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites and spreads to people mainly through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.
