WHO estimates 282 million malaria cases and 610,000 malaria deaths in 2024; 95 percent of the deaths were in the WHO African Region, where children under 5 were about 75 percent of malaria deaths.

title: Arthropods: jointed feet
description: Insects, spiders and crustaceans are arthropods: jointed outer skeletons of chitin and protein, segmented bodies and jointed legs. About 84 percent of described animal species are arthropods; mollusks like snails are not.

facts.text: Arthropods have a jointed outer skeleton of chitin bound to protein and a usually segmented body whose segments bear paired jointed appendages; arthropod means jointed feet. They include insects, spiders and crustaceans.
By Britannica’s count, about 84 percent of the described animal species are arthropods, most of them insects.

title: What an adaptation is
description: An adaptation fits living things to their environment and improves their chances of survival there; it can be a body feature or a behavior. Individuals don't adapt: populations do, over generations.

facts.text: Adaptation is the adjustment of organisms to their environment that improves their chances of survival there; it can be a physical feature or a behavior.
Individual organisms cannot adapt; adaptation happens in populations over several generations, the result of natural selection acting on inherited variation.

title: Two foxes fitted to heat and cold
description: The desert fennec fox has the largest ears for its size in the dog family, which shed heat, plus furry paws and a daytime burrow; the Arctic fox's small ears reduce heat loss.

facts.text: The fennec, a desert fox, has the largest ears relative to body size of any member of the dog family, and they help release body heat to keep it cool.
Fennec foxes have thick-furred paws that protect their feet from hot sand, and they spend the heat of the day in burrows, hunting at night.
The Arctic fox has short, rounded ears, and small ears reduce heat loss because less of the body is exposed to the cold.

title: Camouflage: background matching, countershading and seasonal coats
description: Animals hide by matching their background in color, shape or movement, by countershading (dark back, pale belly) that flattens their look, and by changing coats with the seasons.

facts.text: In background matching, an animal hides by resembling its surroundings in color, form or movement, as deer, squirrels, flounder, walking sticks and walking leaves do.
Leaf insects rock back and forth as they move, mimicking a leaf blown by the wind.
Countershading gives an animal darker upper surfaces than its lower, shaded ones; this evens out light and shadow, so the body looks flatter and is harder to see.
Sharks are countershaded: seen from above, the dark back blends with deep water; seen from below, the pale belly blends with the bright surface.
Many Arctic foxes are white in winter and grayish brown in summer, so their coat matches the season.

title: Warning colors
description: Bold warning coloration (aposematism) advertises that an animal is toxic or dangerous. Monarchs keep milkweed poison in their bodies, and predators learn to avoid the pattern.

facts.text: Monarch caterpillars feed on milkweeds, and the butterflies keep the plants' poisons (cardenolides) in their bodies for protection.
Warning coloration (aposematism) uses bold patterns to make predators aware that an animal is toxic or dangerous.
A predator that has a bad experience with one warning pattern learns to avoid it, and then avoids other species with a similar pattern too.

title: Batesian and Müllerian mimicry
description: In Batesian mimicry a harmless species copies a dangerous one (Bates, 1862); in Müllerian mimicry harmful species share one pattern (Muller, 1878). The viceroy turned out to be Müllerian.

facts.text: In Batesian mimicry a harmless species closely resembles a dangerous, conspicuous one; Henry Walter Bates described it in 1862 from Brazilian butterflies.
The harmless scarlet king snake wears warning colors that mimic those of the venomous coral snake.
In Müllerian mimicry, proposed by Fritz Müller in 1878, harmful or inedible species resemble each other, so they share the cost of teaching predators.
The viceroy looks like a smaller monarch and was long called a Batesian mimic; in 1991 Ritland and Brower found birds judge it about as distasteful as a monarch, so it is Müllerian.
In the 1991 test, red-winged blackbirds were offered butterfly bodies with the wings removed, so they judged by taste alone.

title: Hibernation and torpor
description: Hibernation is a long, deep drop in metabolism and body temperature, with brief wake-ups every few weeks; torpor is the same slowdown on a shorter scale, sometimes just a few hours.

facts.text: Hibernation is greatly reduced metabolism and lowered body temperature in winter; body temperature can fall near 0 °C, with a few breaths a minute and a barely detectable heartbeat.
True hibernators live on stored body fat in a protected den; every few weeks they warm up and wake briefly, then return to torpor.
Hibernating Arctic ground squirrels let their core temperature fall below freezing, as low as −2.9 °C, without freezing (Barnes, 1989).
In torpor an animal's body temperature falls and its cells slow down; white-footed mice and shrews use daily torpor lasting just a few hours.

title: Do bears truly hibernate?
description: Bears cool only a few degrees and wake fairly easily, so Britannica does not count them as true hibernators; a 2011 study found black bears cut metabolism to about 25 percent and called it hibernation.

facts.text: Britannica says bears don't lower their body temperature much and wake fairly easily, so they are not considered true hibernators.
In 2011, a University of Alaska Fairbanks team found hibernating black bears cut metabolism to about 25 percent of normal while cooling only about 5 to 6 °C.
Hibernating black bears go 5 to 7 months without eating, drinking, urinating or defecating.
Whether bears are true hibernators is debated: the 2011 team called it hibernation, while others say bears don't cool enough to qualify.

title: Surviving with little water
description: A camel's hump is fat, not water; it drinks huge amounts at once and can then go nearly a week without. A kangaroo rat makes water from dry seeds and wastes almost none.

facts.text: A camel's hump stores fat, not water, as food for when food is scarce; keeping fat in the hump avoids insulating the rest of the body in the heat.
A camel can drink up to about 30 gallons (about 114 liters) of water in one sitting, and can go nearly a week without drinking.
Kangaroo rats eat mostly dry seeds and get about half a gram of water from each gram, about a drop per two seeds, so they have almost no need to drink.
Kangaroo rats neither sweat nor pant, and their kidneys concentrate their urine to an almost crystal-like consistency, so very little water is lost.
Kangaroo rats stay in their burrows during the day and come out at night to forage.

title: Surviving polar cold
description: Polar bears keep warm with thick fur over black skin, a fat layer and furred soles; penguins trap air in tight feathers over fat, and swap heat between leg arteries and veins so little is lost through the feet.

facts.text: A polar bear's skin is black and its hairs are clear, with no pigment; the fur looks white because light is scattered by the clear hairs.
Polar bears have thick fur and a layer of insulating fat under the skin, which they keep up by eating seal blubber.
The soles of a polar bear's feet are furred, for insulation and for grip on ice and snow.
Penguins' short, stiff feathers are packed tightly and trap a layer of air next to the skin, the main insulation, over a thick layer of fat.
In penguins' legs, arteries and veins run close together, so warm blood heading down passes heat to cold blood coming back, and less is lost through the feet.
An emperor penguin's foot skin stays near 0 °C, so it doesn't melt the ice it stands on.

title: Armor, spines and spray
description: Some animals defend themselves with armor (the three-banded armadillo rolls into a ball), spines (porcupine quills that detach in an attacker) or chemicals (the skunk's aimed spray, announced by a warning).

facts.text: The southern three-banded armadillo has leathery armor plates and can roll completely into a ball; only the Brazilian three-banded armadillo can too.
Rolled into a ball, a three-banded armadillo shields its soft belly inside its armor.
A North American porcupine has about 30,000 quills; they are never thrown or shot, but are so lightly attached that they come off easily in an attacker.
A cornered porcupine raises its quills, turns its back to the attacker and lashes its tail; quills in skin work deeper at about 1 mm an hour.
A striped skunk warns first by stomping its feet and raising its tail; then it can spray about 10 feet (3 meters) with startling accuracy.
A skunk needs about a week to refill its spray, and its white stripes are warning coloration.

title: Seeing in the dark
description: Nocturnal animals are active after dark to hunt, mate or avoid daytime heat and predators. Many have enlarged eyes, and many have a tapetum lucidum, a mirror behind the retina that causes eyeshine; tarsiers lack one and have huge eyes instead.

facts.text: Nocturnal animals are active after dark: to hunt, to find mates, or to avoid the heat and the predators of the day.
Many nocturnal animals have enlarged eyes with wide pupils that collect more light.
Many nocturnal vertebrates, such as cats and crocodiles, have a tapetum lucidum: a layer behind the retina that reflects light back for a second chance, causing eyeshine.
Tarsiers are nocturnal primates whose eyes are so big that one weighs nearly as much as the brain; they lack the tapetum most nocturnal mammals have.

title: Senses we lack
description: Sharks and rays sense electric fields, pit vipers sense infrared heat, sea turtles navigate by Earth's magnetic field, and reindeer see ultraviolet light.

facts.text: Sharks and rays sense the weak electric fields of prey, even prey buried in sand, with organs called ampullae of Lorenzini; humans have no electroreceptors.
Pit vipers such as rattlesnakes have a heat-sensitive pit between each eye and nostril that senses infrared from warm-blooded prey, aiding strikes in darkness.
Sea turtles use Earth's magnetic field to navigate long migrations; loggerhead hatchlings swim different ways in the magnetic fields of different places on their route.
Reindeer can see ultraviolet light, which human lenses block; against snow, UV-absorbing lichen (winter food), urine and wolf fur look dark (UCL, 2011).

title: The wood frog freezes and thaws
description: Wood frogs survive winter with about 65 percent of the body frozen: glucose keeps the inside of the cells unfrozen while the water outside turns to ice, the heart stops, and the frog thaws in spring.

facts.text: Wood frogs winter in leaf litter and can survive with about 65 percent of their bodies frozen; their hearts stop and organs shut down until they thaw.
A freezing wood frog's liver fills its cells with glucose, which keeps the inside of the cells from freezing while water outside them turns to ice.
When it warms, a wood frog thaws from the inside out, starting with the heart.

title: Instinct and learning
description: Instincts are innate behaviors performed without practice, like a gull chick pecking at the red spot on its parent's bill. Learned behaviors are shaped by experience, like prairie dogs tuning out harmless footsteps. Most behavior mixes both.

facts.text: Innate behaviors (instincts) have a strong genetic component and are largely independent of the environment, so there is no risk of learning them wrong; learned behaviors are flexible and change with experience.
Newly hatched herring gull chicks peck at the red spot on the parent's bill, which makes the parent regurgitate food for them.
Prairie dogs give alarm calls at threats but become habituated to the sound of human footsteps that bring no harm, while still calling at predators.
No behavior is strictly innate or entirely learned: all behavior results from an interaction between genes and the environment.

title: Imprinting
description: Imprinting is fast learning in an early critical period: a hatchling learns to follow the first moving thing it sees. Lorenz's ducklings followed him; Tex the whooping crane imprinted on people, so crane chicks are now raised by keepers in crane costumes.

facts.text: Imprinting is learning during an early critical period of life: a newly hatched duckling learns to follow the first moving object it sees, whether its mother, a person or a cardboard box.
In 1935, Konrad Lorenz imitated a mother duck's quacking in front of newly hatched mallard ducklings, and they treated him as their mother.
Tex, a whooping crane hatched at the San Antonio Zoo and raised around people in the 1970s, imprinted on humans and would not pair with another whooping crane.
Starting in spring 1976, George Archibald danced with Tex the way a male whooping crane courts, since dancing is how whooping cranes begin mating; in 1982 Tex hatched a chick named Gee Whiz.
Keepers raising whooping crane chicks wear crane costumes with a crane hand puppet so the chicks imprint on whooping cranes rather than on people.

title: How animals send signals
description: A signal is information one animal gives off that another can use to decide what to do. Signals travel by smell (pheromones), sound, sight and touch; displays can even replace a fight.

facts.text: Animal communication is the process by which one animal provides information that other animals can use in their decision making.
Animal signals can be chemical (pheromones), sound, visual displays or touch, such as grooming among primates; they may be instinctive, learned or a mix of both.
A pheromone is a chemical signal an animal releases to get a response from another member of its own species, used for example to attract mates, sound alarms or mark food trails.
Aggressive displays, like a dog baring its teeth, let rivals judge each other's fighting ability and so reduce actual fighting; some displays overstate strength as a bluff.

title: Vervet monkey alarm calls
description: Vervet monkeys give different alarm calls for leopards, eagles and snakes. Played back with no predator present, each call still triggers the right escape.

facts.text: Vervet monkeys give acoustically different alarm calls to leopards, eagles and snakes.

In a 1980 study in Amboseli, Kenya, Robert Seyfarth, Dorothy Cheney and Peter Marler played recorded alarm calls with no predator present: monkeys ran into trees for leopard alarms, looked up for eagle alarms and looked down for snake alarms.

title: The honeybee waggle dance
description: A forager does a round dance for food near the hive and a waggle dance for food farther away. The waggle run's angle from straight up on the comb gives the direction relative to the sun; its duration gives the distance.

facts.text: Karl von Frisch showed how honeybees share where food is: a forager that finds food near the hive performs a round dance, which sends nestmates searching nearby; for food farther away she performs a waggle dance, running straight while waggling her abdomen, then looping back to repeat.
On the vertical comb, straight up stands for the direction of the sun: the angle of the waggle run from vertical equals the angle of the food from the sun.
The duration of the waggle run encodes distance: the longer it lasts, the farther away the food.
Honeybees can use the sun as a compass even when it is hidden, by perceiving polarized light.

title: Decoding the bee dance
description: Karl von Frisch decoded the bee dance and shared the 1973 Nobel Prize with Lorenz and Tinbergen. The 1973 view was that the dance is inborn; a 2023 study showed young bees also learn it from experienced dancers.

facts.text: Karl von Frisch, Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries about individual and social behavior patterns; the prize committee called them founders of ethology, the study of animal behavior.
The 1973 Nobel announcement described the bee's dance communication as genetically programmed and not learned.

A 2023 study found that honeybees unable to follow experienced dancers before their own first dance made more disordered dances and encoded distance incorrectly; practice helped, but they never got distance right.

title: Why animals live in groups
description: Groups dilute each member's risk, confuse predators and help hunters corner prey. They also cost something: competition for food, and a crowd can draw predators.

facts.text: When a predator takes one prey per attack, each group member's risk falls with group size (from p to p/N): in a group of 100, 1 in 100; animals inside a group, like a fish school, are safer still, and groups can confuse predators by scattering.
Predators that cooperate, such as lions, hyenas and wolves, can corner and bring down prey more easily.
Group living has costs: members compete for the same food, and if a group attracts too many predators, an individual may be better off alone.

title: Wolf packs are families
description: The "alpha wolf" came from captive packs of unrelated wolves. In the wild, L. David Mech found, a pack is a family: a breeding pair and their young, led by the parents.

facts.text: The alpha-wolf picture came mostly from studies of captive wolves, such as Schenkel's in 1947, where unrelated wolves thrown together formed dominance hierarchies.
In 1999, L. David Mech of the U.S. Geological Survey concluded that a typical wild wolf pack is a family: a breeding pair and their offspring from the previous 1 to 3 years.
Mech himself had once used terms like alpha and beta; he now compares calling a wolf an alpha to calling a human father one.

In 13 summers watching a wild pack on Ellesmere Island, Canada, Mech saw no dominance contests; the mother mainly cared for and defended pups, the father mainly led hunting and food delivery, and dominance displays showed up mostly over food, which parents steered to the youngest.

title: Mate choice
description: In many species one sex chooses and the other competes to be chosen. Peahens favor the most showy peacocks, so traits that win mates spread even when they make survival harder.

facts.text: Peahens tend to choose to mate with the peacock showing the brightest, most elaborate plumage.
Mate choice can favor traits that do not help survival, or even cost it, because they attract the opposite sex.

title: Courtship signals
description: Courtship runs on signals: songs that name the species and draw mates, displays performed step by step, and the satin bowerbird's decorated stage of sticks.

facts.text: Birdsong identifies the singer's species and is used to attract mates.
Courtship displays often run as a series of steps, a display by one partner followed by a response from the other; if a step goes wrong or the response never comes, the courtship is abandoned.

The male satin bowerbird of Australia builds a bower of two parallel walls of sticks on the ground and decorates it with blue objects such as bottle tops, drinking straws, clothes pegs, parrot feathers and flowers; he paints the walls with chewed plant matter and saliva.

When a female arrives, the male satin bowerbird struts and bows with quivering wings, buzzing and rattling, often holding a decoration in his bill; if she mates, she then builds a nest and raises the young on her own.

title: The price of parental care
description: Care costs future offspring, so animals trade many young with little care against few young with a lot. Mammal mothers carry and nurse their young; orangutans sit at the extreme.

facts.text: Parental care costs future reproduction: a female guarding one clutch of eggs does so at the expense of laying another.
Mammal mothers feed their young milk, and in placental mammals the mother first carries her young through pregnancy.
Orangutan infants cling to their mothers from birth and can nurse until they are 6 or 7 years old; a mother has a baby only about every 7 to 9 years, so only 4 or 5 in her lifetime.
Young female orangutans may stay with their mothers into their teens, watching younger siblings being raised and so observing mothering skills.

title: Seahorse fathers
description: Male-only care is rare. In seahorses and pipefishes the male carries the eggs: the female places them in his brood pouch, and he gives birth to young that get no further care.

facts.text: A female seahorse places her eggs in a brood pouch at the base of the male's tail; he carries them for between 10 days and six weeks, depending on the species, then pushes the young out through an opening in the pouch, and they receive no further care.
Care by the male alone is rare in animals, but seahorse and pipefish males carry the eggs and brood the young.

title: What counts as a tool
description: In 1960 Jane Goodall saw chimpanzees use and make tools to fish for termites, overturning the idea that only humans do. A tool pays off only when it is used for a job, which is why a hermit crab's shell doesn't count.

facts.text: In 1960, at Gombe in Tanzania, Jane Goodall watched a chimpanzee she named David Greybeard poke grass into a termite mound and then raise it to his mouth; soon after, she saw chimps strip the leaves off leafy twigs to use as tools, object modification never seen before.
Before Goodall's discovery, making and using tools was thought to set humans apart; Louis Leakey responded that we must now redefine man or accept chimpanzees as human.

Biologists counted the octopus's coconut shell as a tool because it gives only delayed benefits, useful once the animal needs shelter; a hermit crab's shell is not a tool, because it is always useful.

title: Tool users beyond chimps
description: Sea otters crack prey with rocks, which spares their teeth; veined octopuses carry coconut shells to build shelters later, the first known tool use by an invertebrate.

facts.text: A 2024 study that followed 196 radio-tagged southern sea otters in California found they use rocks, shells and even trash to break open prey; tool users, mostly females, could eat harder and larger prey and had less tooth damage.
For a sea otter, badly worn teeth can mean starvation; researchers think females use tools to make up for smaller bodies and weaker bites, because raising pups takes a lot of energy.

Veined octopuses in Indonesia dig up coconut shell halves, carry them beneath their bodies while walking awkwardly on stiffened arms, and later put them together as a shelter; reported in 2009, it was the first known tool use by an invertebrate.

title: The mirror mark test
description: Gordon Gallup Jr.'s 1970 test puts a mark where an animal can see it only in a mirror. Great apes, dolphins, elephants and magpies have passed, but often only some individuals.

facts.text: In 1970, psychologist Gordon Gallup Jr. developed the mirror test: chimpanzees marked with red dye used a mirror to examine the marks on their own bodies.

In the mark test, animals first get used to the mirror (many attack their reflection), then often make unusual movements as if testing the image, and finally get a colored mark; poking at the mark while watching the reflection counts as recognizing themselves.
Great apes, dolphins, elephants and magpies are among the few animals that have passed the mirror mark test.

In a 2006 Bronx Zoo study of three Asian elephants, only Happy clearly passed: she repeatedly touched a white X painted on one side of her head, while an invisible mark on the other side checked that she wasn't reacting to feel or smell.

title: Limits of the mirror test
description: The mirror test is a sight test. Dogs, who live by smell, fail it but react to changes in their own scent; a fish that passed was doubted even by the test's inventor.

facts.text: Dogs rely mainly on smell rather than sight; in a 2017 smell-based version of the test, dogs sniffed their own urine longer when an extra odor had been added to it.
In 2019, cleaner wrasse fish scraped at marks seen only in a mirror, but Gallup doubted the result: the fish might simply have been reacting to what looked like a parasite.

title: Play signals and fair play
description: Canids ask to play with a bow, a signal used almost only in play. Players keep it fair by holding back and letting the other win sometimes.

facts.text: Dogs, wolves and coyotes invite play with a bow, crouching on their forelimbs while standing on their hind legs; the bow is used almost only in play and always looks the same; after a bow, rough moves like growling or biting draw submission or avoidance only about 15 percent of the time.

Playing animals keep things fair: a stronger coyote may not bite as hard as it can, a dominant animal may roll onto its back to let a weaker partner win, and young rats with the upper hand often give it up the same way.

title: Why young animals play
description: Play looks useless and costs energy. It may not be simple practice: young elk never head-butt in play. Rats deprived of play grow up anxious and socially clumsy, so play seems to train social judgment.

facts.text: Play has no obvious immediate purpose, yet it costs energy and is noisy and conspicuous: play-fighting rats could draw a hungry hawk.
Play fighting often avoids real fighting moves: young elk lock horns in play but never butt heads, a move saved for serious fights.
Young rats deprived of play fighting grow up anxious and overreact to other rats, and later handle courtship poorly; researchers think play trains the brain to adjust behavior to the situation.

title: Key stimuli and supernormal stimuli
description: Instincts are triggered by a few key features. Tinbergen tested gull chicks with dummy bills and found that exaggerating those features makes a supernormal stimulus that beats the real thing.

facts.text: Nikolaas Tinbergen used dummies to test which features of a gull's bill, such as its shape, colors and contrasts, trigger a chick's begging pecks.
By exaggerating certain features, Tinbergen produced supernormal (supranormal) stimuli: fakes that trigger a stronger response than the natural stimulus.
Lorenz found that many instinctive acts are fixed action patterns set off only by specific key stimuli, which naive young animals respond to without any experience.

title: Darwin's voyage on the Beagle
description: From 1831 to 1836, the young Charles Darwin sailed around the world on HMS Beagle, collecting animals, plants and fossils. In South America he dug up giant ground sloths like Megatherium, extinct giants related to living sloths.

facts.text: Charles Darwin, born in 1809, sailed from England on HMS Beagle in December 1831, aged 22, as a companion to its captain, Robert FitzRoy; the voyage lasted five years, ending in 1836.
On the Beagle voyage, Darwin collected plants, animals and fossils and took copious field notes.
In Argentina, Darwin dug up fossil skulls, thighbones and armor plates, including remains of giant ground sloths such as Megatherium, which weighed up to four tonnes yet was related to modern sloths.

title: Island-to-island differences in the Galápagos
description: In the Galápagos, Darwin noticed mockingbirds differed from island to island. John Gould later showed they were separate species, and that Darwin's mixed bag of birds were all ground finches, which set Darwin wondering how they diverged. He published his theory in 1859.

facts.text: Darwin reached the Galápagos Islands in September 1835; he noticed the mockingbirds differed on four islands and labeled them by island, but failed to label his other birds, including finches, by island.

In 1837 the ornithologist John Gould reported that the Galápagos mockingbirds were three species unique to different islands, and that the birds Darwin took for wrens, finches and 'gross-beaks' were all ground finches; Darwin began asking how they had diverged from mainland colonists.
Darwin set out his theory of evolution by natural selection in On the Origin of Species, published in 1859.

title: How natural selection works
description: Natural selection needs three things: variation among individuals, differences in how many offspring they leave, and heredity. Given those, advantageous traits become more common over generations.

facts.text: Evolution by natural selection follows whenever a population has variation, differential reproduction and heredity; in UE's example, birds eat more green beetles than brown ones, the survivors pass on their color, and brown becomes more common.

The National Academies define natural selection as the process by which organisms with advantageous variations have greater reproductive success than others in a population; over generations, populations can change.

title: The Grants' finches: selection seen in two years
description: On Daphne Major, Peter and Rosemary Grant saw a 1977 drought kill most medium ground finches; birds with larger beaks, able to crack big seeds, survived, and their offspring inherited larger beaks. Later rains reversed the trend.

facts.text: Peter and Rosemary Grant began studying Darwin's finches on the Galápagos island of Daphne Major in 1973, catching and measuring the birds; they expected a two-year project and kept going for 40 years.

In early 1977 only 24 millimeters of rain fell on Daphne Major; small seeds grew scarce, most of the finches died, and the medium ground finches that survived, a species with short beaks suited to small seeds, were those with larger beaks able to crack larger seeds.
Beak size is heritable, so the following generations of medium ground finches on Daphne Major had measurably larger beaks: natural selection and evolution witnessed over just two years.
After heavy rains in 1982-83 brought plentiful small seeds, medium ground finches with smaller beaks fed more efficiently, and the average beak size moved back down.

title: How fossils form
description: Fossils are rare: most dead things rot away. Quick burial in sediment is key, which is why around 99% of fossils are sea animals. In petrification, minerals left by water turn buried bones to stone. Body fossils are remains; trace fossils are signs like footprints.

facts.text: A fossil is physical evidence of a prehistoric plant or animal: body fossils are preserved remains such as bones, teeth and shells, while trace fossils are signs such as footprints, skin impressions and fossil dung (coprolites).

Fossilisation is rare: most things that die rot away completely, and around 99% of fossils found are from sea animals such as shellfish and sharks, because sand or mud could bury their remains quickly.

In petrification, an animal's soft parts rot, often leaving only bones and teeth; sediment such as mud, sand or silt buries them; more layers press down and become sedimentary rock; and water seeping in leaves minerals that turn the bones to stone, over thousands or millions of years.

title: Reading the age of fossils from rock layers
description: In undisturbed rock, lower layers were laid down first, so their fossils are older (superposition). Radiometric dating of volcanic ash above and below a fossil brackets its age, and comparing layers worldwide built the geologic timescale.

facts.text: In undisturbed rock layers, fossils in lower layers were deposited earlier and are older than fossils in higher layers; this principle is called superposition.

Radioactive elements decay at measured rates, so dating volcanic ash layers above and below a fossil gives its age range; in one example, trilobites were shown to be older than 520 but younger than 545 million years.
By comparing rock layers and their fossils from all over the world, paleontologists established the geologic timescale, which orders the events of life's history.

title: When dinosaurs lived
description: Non-bird dinosaurs lived from about 245 to 66 million years ago, in the Mesozoic Era: the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous periods. The span was so long that Stegosaurus was long extinct before Tyrannosaurus appeared.

facts.text: Non-bird dinosaurs lived between about 245 and 66 million years ago, in the Mesozoic Era; the first dinosaurs appeared in the Triassic Period, around 245 million years ago.
The Mesozoic Era is divided into three periods: the Triassic (252 to 201 million years ago), the Jurassic (201 to 145 million years ago) and the Cretaceous (145 to 66 million years ago).

The Jurassic dinosaur Stegosaurus had been extinct for about 80 million years before the Cretaceous dinosaur Tyrannosaurus appeared: more time separates Stegosaurus and Tyrannosaurus than Tyrannosaurus and you.

title: Why dinosaurs became so varied
description: Dinosaurs began on one supercontinent, Pangaea. As it split apart, dinosaurs on separate continents evolved independently and became more diverse, from Jurassic sauropods to Cretaceous titanosaurs.

facts.text: In the Triassic all continents formed one landmass, Pangaea, so animals in different areas differed little; as it broke apart, dinosaurs were scattered on separate continents and new types evolved separately, becoming more diverse.

Plentiful Jurassic plants allowed huge plant-eating sauropods such as Diplodocus and Brachiosaurus, some of the largest animals ever to walk the Earth, to evolve; sauropods reached their largest sizes in the Cretaceous, where the biggest were the titanosaurs.
A mass extinction at the end of the Triassic wiped out many large land animals, but the dinosaurs survived, giving them the opportunity to evolve into a wide variety of forms.

title: Birds descend from theropod dinosaurs
description: Birds evolved from small meat-eating theropod dinosaurs, the group that includes T. rex. Feathered non-bird dinosaurs like Sinosauropteryx show feathers came before birds, and when the other dinosaurs died out, birds survived: they are living dinosaurs.

facts.text: Birds evolved from small theropods, the group of meat-eating dinosaurs that Tyrannosaurus rex belonged to; the oldest bird-like fossils are more than 150 million years old and had sharp teeth, and birds later lost their teeth and evolved beaks.
At the end-Cretaceous extinction 66 million years ago, all the non-bird dinosaurs died out, but dinosaurs survived as birds.

Sinosauropteryx, a small meat-eating theropod from China found in 1996, had a covering of thin, hair-like primitive feathers; it was the first feathered dinosaur discovered that was not directly related to birds.

title: Archaeopteryx, part bird and part dinosaur
description: Archaeopteryx, about 150 million years old and found in Germany from 1861, had feathers like a bird but teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail like small theropod dinosaurs.

facts.text: Archaeopteryx fossils, about 150 million years old (Late Jurassic), have been found in the Solnhofen Limestone of Bavaria, Germany, starting in 1861.

Archaeopteryx had feathers, but unlike living birds it had well-developed teeth, three clawed fingers and a long bony tail like smaller dinosaurs; it shared many features with coelurosaurs, a group of theropods.

title: The Big Five mass extinctions
description: Most species that ever lived are extinct, and five times the fossil record shows mass extinctions: the Ordovician-Silurian, Late Devonian, end-Permian (the worst, about 90 percent of species), end-Triassic and end-Cretaceous.

facts.text: The vast majority of species ever to have lived are extinct.

The five major mass extinctions are the Ordovician-Silurian (about 444 million years ago), the Late Devonian (about 372 million years ago), the end-Permian (about 252 million years ago), the end-Triassic (about 201 million years ago) and the end-Cretaceous (about 66 million years ago).
The end-Permian extinction was the most severe in the fossil record, eliminating about 90 percent of all species.

title: The asteroid that ended the non-bird dinosaurs
description: In 1980 the Alvarezes linked a worldwide iridium-rich clay layer to an asteroid impact. The Chicxulub crater on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula matches the extinction's age, 66 million years ago, and the impact is the most widely accepted cause.

facts.text: In 1980, physicist Luis Alvarez and his geologist son Walter proposed that an iridium-rich clay layer, found around the world at the end of the Cretaceous, was caused by a large asteroid impact; iridium is rare on Earth but more abundant in meteorites.

The impact site, the Chicxulub crater, is centred on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula and is the same age as the extinction of the non-bird dinosaurs, 66 million years ago; the asteroid was about 10 to 15 km wide.

The Alvarez asteroid hypothesis was controversial at first but is now the most widely accepted explanation for the end-Cretaceous mass extinction; volcanic eruptions in India (the Deccan Traps) were already stressing life, and the asteroid was the final blow.

The asteroid vaporised on impact and threw debris and soot into the atmosphere, cutting the sunlight reaching the surface and so plant growth; less plant life hurt herbivores and then carnivores, collapsing ecosystems.

title: Tiktaalik: from water toward land
description: Tiktaalik, a 375-million-year-old fish from Arctic Canada, had scales, gills and fin rays, but also a neck, shoulders, thick ribs and sturdy wrist bones. It shows the transition from fish to four-legged vertebrates.

facts.text: Tiktaalik roseae, a 375-million-year-old fossil fish, was found in 2004 on Ellesmere Island in Arctic Canada by a team led by Neil Shubin, Edward Daeschler and Farish Jenkins.
Tiktaalik had scales, gills and fins with thin ray bones like a fish, but also a flattened crocodile-like head, a neck, shoulders, thick ribs and sturdy wrist bones like a four-legged vertebrate.

Tiktaalik's sturdy fin bones would have let it prop itself up in shallow water, and its neck let it turn its head while its body rested on the bottom; its shoulder, elbow and wrist are made of the same bones as our upper arm, forearm and wrist.
Neil Shubin said that every time you bend your wrists, you can thank fish that lived in streams 375 million years ago.
Tiktaalik shows the evolutionary transition between swimming fish and the four-legged vertebrates, a group that includes amphibians, dinosaurs, birds, mammals and humans.

title: Tiktaalik as a confirmed prediction
description: Evidence suggested vertebrates moved onto land about 375 million years ago, so Shubin's team searched rocks of that age from an ancient river delta and found Tiktaalik. The National Academy of Sciences cites it as a prediction of evolutionary theory that came true.

facts.text: Earlier research suggested vertebrates moved onto land about 375 million years ago, so Tiktaalik's discoverers searched 375-million-year-old rocks that preserved a river delta; the National Academy of Sciences cites the find as a prediction of evolutionary theory confirmed.

title: Whales evolved from land mammals
description: Whales' ancestors walked on land about 50 million years ago. Pakicetus lived at the water's edge on four legs; Ambulocetus had paddle-like feet and swam with its tail; Dorudon had flippers and tiny hind legs and lived entirely in water.

facts.text: Whales' land-dwelling ancestors lived about 50 million years ago; Pakicetus, a four-legged animal recognised as one of the first cetaceans, lived on land at the edges of lakes and rivers in what is now Pakistan and India.

Ambulocetus lived in or near estuaries about 50 to 48 million years ago; it spent time in and out of water, had large paddle-like feet and used its tail for swimming, and oxygen isotopes in its bones show it drank both salt water and fresh water.
Dorudon, which lived 40 to 33 million years ago, had flippers and tiny hind legs and lived entirely in the water; about 34 million years ago baleen whales, which include blue whales, evolved.

title: Clues to whales' land ancestry
description: Pakicetus looked like a land mammal but had a whale-like inner ear region. Whales beat their tails up and down because their land-mammal ancestors' backbones bent that way, and hippos are their closest living relatives, cousins rather than ancestors.

facts.text: Pakicetus looked like a typical land mammal, with a long skull and large meat-eating teeth, but its skull's inner ear region, surrounded by a bony wall, strongly resembles living whales' and is unlike any other mammal's.
Whales swim by moving their tails up and down rather than side to side like fish, because they evolved from walking land mammals whose backbones bend up and down, as a running dog's does.
Hippos are whales' closest living relatives but not their ancestors; the ancestors of both groups lived on land.

title: The peppered moth and industrial soot
description: Dark peppered moths, first noticed in Manchester in 1848, took over as soot blackened trees and killed pale lichens, because birds found light moths more easily. After the air was cleaned up, the dark form declined.

facts.text: A dark (melanic) form of the peppered moth was first noticed in Manchester, England, in 1848; by 1898 dark moths there outnumbered light ones 99 to 1.

Peppered moths rest on tree bark by day; in the Industrial Revolution coal soot covered the trees and killed light-coloured lichens, so dark moths were less conspicuous to birds, and birds ate more light moths and fewer dark ones.
Since about 1970, as the air became less sooty, dark peppered moths in Britain have rapidly become rarer again.

title: Majerus's experiment confirms bird predation
description: After critics questioned earlier experiments, Michael Majerus released 4,864 moths near Cambridge over six years. Birds ate dark moths more often, enough to explain their decline. Colleagues published his results in 2012, the most direct evidence yet for camouflage and bird predation.

facts.text: After the classic explanation of the peppered moth was attacked and some doubted birds were the cause, Michael Majerus released 4,864 moths near Cambridge over six years, the largest such experiment, letting them settle naturally at low density and watching birds prey on them.

Majerus found strong bird predation against dark peppered moths, enough to explain their recent decline in Britain: the most direct evidence yet that camouflage and bird predation explain the rise and fall of the dark form.
Majerus died in 2009 before publishing; Laurence Cook, Bruce Grant, Ilik Saccheri and James Mallet analysed his results and published them in Biology Letters in 2012.

title: What "theory" means in science
description: In everyday talk a theory is a hunch; in science it is a comprehensive explanation of part of nature backed by a vast body of evidence. The National Academy of Sciences says there is no scientific controversy about the basic facts of evolution.

facts.text: In everyday use 'theory' often means a hunch, but the scientific meaning is a comprehensive explanation of some aspect of nature supported by a vast body of evidence, such as the theory that living things are made of cells.
The National Academy of Sciences says there is no scientific controversy about the basic facts of evolution, which has withstood testing by many thousands of scientists for more than a century.

title: Domestication versus taming
description: Domestication changes a line of animals by selective breeding over generations, often choosing calmer animals; taming changes only one animal's behavior. Dogs were the first animals domesticated, by hunter-gatherers.

facts.text: Domestication is a hereditary change in wild animals, bred by people over many generations; taming changes one animal's behavior, not its heredity.
Selecting animals for docility and tameness has been central to domestication.
Dogs were the first animals to be domesticated, by hunter-gatherers, before farming began.

title: How cattle and horses were domesticated
description: All domestic cattle trace back to about 80 aurochs domesticated about 10,500 years ago in the Near East; the wild aurochs died out in 1627. Modern domestic horses come from the lower Volga-Don steppe around 2200 BCE and carry changes linked to docility and a stronger backbone.

facts.text: Ancient DNA from cattle bones found in Iran suggests all domestic cattle descend from about 80 aurochs, wild oxen domesticated about 10,500 years ago in the Near East; keeping aurochs captive was hard.
The aurochs, the wild ox from which cattle are probably descended, survived in central Poland until 1627.

Ancient DNA from 273 horses shows modern domestic horses began on the western Eurasian steppes, especially the lower Volga-Don region, around 2200 BCE, then spread across Eurasia, replacing other horses.
Two genetic changes stand out in the horses that spread: one linked to more docile behavior and one indicating a stronger backbone.

title: Farm animals outweigh wild ones
description: By carbon mass, livestock make up about 60% of Earth's mammals, people about 36% and wild mammals about 4%; domestic poultry has almost three times the mass of all wild birds (2018 estimate).

facts.text: A 2018 census of life by carbon mass found livestock, mostly cattle and pigs, make up about 60 percent of mammals, humans about 36 percent and wild mammals about 4 percent.
The same 2018 census found domestic poultry, mainly chickens, have almost three times the biomass of all wild birds.

title: Where farm animals came from and what they give
description: Chickens come from the red junglefowl and may first have been kept for fighting or religion. Cattle give meat, milk, hides and pulling power; high milk yields came from later breeding. Cattle, sheep and goats are ruminants that chew cud because they cannot digest cellulose directly.

facts.text: Chickens descend from the wild red junglefowl of Asia, and their first domestications may have been for religious reasons or for fighting birds rather than food.
Cattle are raised for meat, milk, hides or pulling loads; early domestic cattle gave only enough milk for their calves, and high milk yields came much later through selective breeding.
Cattle, sheep and goats are ruminants: they cannot digest the cellulose in grass and leaves directly, so they bring food back up as cud and chew it again.

title: The IUCN Red List
description: The IUCN Red List sorts assessed species from Least Concern to Extinct; Vulnerable, Endangered and Critically Endangered count as threatened. In version 2025-1, 47,187 of 169,420 evaluated species were threatened, including about 41% of amphibians; only about 1% of insects had been evaluated.

facts.text: The IUCN Red List categories run Least Concern, Near Threatened, Vulnerable, Endangered, Critically Endangered, Extinct in the Wild and Extinct, plus Data Deficient and Not Evaluated.
On the IUCN Red List, threatened species are those listed as Critically Endangered, Endangered or Vulnerable.
In IUCN Red List version 2025-1 (March 2025), 169,420 species had been evaluated and 47,187 of them were threatened with extinction.
IUCN's best estimates in Red List version 2025-1: about 41 percent of amphibian species and 27 percent of mammal species are threatened.
By Red List version 2025-1, only about 1 percent of described insect species (13,442 of about 1 million, or 1.3 percent) had been evaluated.

title: Why species become endangered
description: Habitat loss is the most pervasive threat to species, alongside introduced species, climate change, pollution, overhunting and disease. The giant panda's biggest threat is habitat destruction; in 2016 IUCN moved it from Endangered to Vulnerable.

facts.text: Habitat loss and degradation, driven by farming, logging and building, is the most pervasive threat to species; others include introduced species, climate change, pollution, overhunting and disease.
Habitat destruction is the giant panda's largest threat: logging and clearing for farms broke its forest into fragments, isolating small groups; as few as 1,864 live in the wild.
In September 2016, IUCN moved the giant panda from Endangered to Vulnerable on the Red List.

title: The dodo and the passenger pigeon
description: The dodo, a flightless relative of pigeons found only on Mauritius, was hunted and preyed on by animals sailors brought, and was gone by the late 1600s. Passenger pigeons numbered 3 to 5 billion but were slaughtered for markets; the last, Martha, died in 1914.

facts.text: The dodo was a flightless bird found only on Mauritius, an island in the Indian Ocean, and is classified with the pigeons.
Sailors hunted dodos, and animals they brought, such as pigs, dogs, cats and rats, preyed on them; the dodo was extinct by the late 1600s (by 1681, per Britannica).
When Europeans arrived in North America there were an estimated 3 to 5 billion passenger pigeons; migrating flocks darkened the skies for days.
Passenger pigeons were slaughtered by the millions each year and shipped by the railway carload to city markets.
Martha, the last known passenger pigeon, died on September 1, 1914, at the Cincinnati Zoo; her body was frozen in a block of ice and sent to the Smithsonian.

title: The thylacine
description: The thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, was the largest meat-eating marsupial of recent times. Hunted as a threat to sheep, with a bounty from 1888 to 1909, it was protected in July 1936; the last known one died at Hobart Zoo on 7 September 1936.

facts.text: The thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, was the largest carnivorous marsupial of recent times, with dark stripes across its back; in historic times it lived only in Tasmania.
Tasmanian settlers hunted the thylacine as a threat to their sheep, and the government paid a bounty on thylacines from 1888 to 1909.
Thylacines were given full protection in July 1936; two months later, on 7 September 1936, the last known thylacine died at Hobart Zoo.

title: How the bald eagle recovered
description: DDT passed from water to fish to bald eagles and thinned their eggshells; by 1963 only 417 nesting pairs were known in the lower 48 states. After the 1972 DDT ban, eagles recovered and left the endangered list in 2007; USFWS estimates about 316,700 today.

facts.text: DDT washed into waterways, was absorbed by water plants and fish, and poisoned bald eagles that ate the fish; it made their eggshells so thin that they often broke during incubation.
By 1963, only 417 nesting pairs of bald eagles were known in the lower 48 United States.
The US Environmental Protection Agency banned DDT in 1972, and the bald eagle was removed from the list of threatened and endangered species in 2007.
A USFWS estimate from 2018 and 2019 surveys counts about 316,700 bald eagles in the lower 48 states, including 71,467 breeding pairs.

title: The California condor and the humpback whale
description: By 1987 every wild California condor was in captive breeding; releases began in 1992 and there are now more than 500, though lead remains the top known killer. Humpbacks recovered after the 1985 whaling moratorium; in 2016 NOAA found 9 of 14 populations no longer needed listing.

facts.text: With a wingspan of 9.5 feet, the California condor is the largest land bird in North America.
By 1987, all remaining wild California condors had been placed in a captive breeding program; captive-bred condors have been released since 1992, and the total population is now more than 500.
Lead poisoning, from fragments of lead ammunition that scavenging condors swallow, is the number one known cause of death in California condors.
Before a final moratorium on commercial whaling in 1985, all humpback whale populations were greatly reduced, most by more than 95 percent.
In 2016 NOAA Fisheries divided humpback whales into 14 distinct populations: 9 no longer warrant listing, 4 are endangered and 1 is threatened.

title: What makes a species invasive
description: An invasive species causes ecological or economic harm in a place where it is not native. Most are moved by people. Invasives can compete with natives, change habitats and drive native species extinct.

facts.text: An invasive species is an organism that causes ecological or economic harm in a new environment where it is not native; most often, people introduce them, on purpose or by accident.
Invasive species can compete with native organisms for limited resources, alter habitats and cause extinctions of native plants and animals.

title: Cane toads and brown treesnakes
description: Cane toads released in Queensland in 1935 to eat cane beetles barely affected the beetles but spread in the millions and poison native predators. Brown treesnakes that reached Guam in cargo helped wipe out 9 of its 11 native forest bird species.

facts.text: In 1935, 2,400 cane toads were released on sugarcane farms in Queensland, Australia, to control beetles attacking the crop; they had little or no effect on the beetles.
Cane toads now number in the millions across northeastern Australia and are advancing west about 40 to 60 km a year; their poison kills many native predators that eat them.
The brown treesnake, native to places including New Guinea and Australia, reached Guam hidden in cargo during or soon after World War II and helped wipe out 9 of Guam's 11 native forest bird species.
Brown treesnakes on Guam crawl on electrical lines and cause expensive power outages.

title: What modern zoos try to do
description: AZA says conservation is central to accredited zoos; its Species Survival Plans (since 1981) combine breeding, habitat protection, education and research. The Arabian oryx, Extinct in the Wild by 1972, was brought back from zoo and royal herds and moved to Vulnerable in 2011.

facts.text: The Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) says conservation is key to accredited zoos' mission; its Species Survival Plans, begun in 1981, combine breeding, habitat protection, education, field work and research.
Uncontrolled hunting made the Arabian oryx Extinct in the Wild; the last wild one is believed to have been shot in Oman in 1972.
Some of the last Arabian oryx were captured to form a 'World Herd', begun at the Phoenix Zoo with nine animals; with royal herds in Arabia, it supplied oryx for reintroduction.
Oryx were first reintroduced in Oman in 1982, then elsewhere; by 2011 about 1,000 lived wild, and IUCN moved them to Vulnerable, the first once Extinct in the Wild species to climb three categories.

title: The debate over zoos
description: AZA argues accredited zoos are conservation centers. Animal-welfare groups such as the Born Free Foundation argue most zoo species are not threatened, few zoo animals return to the wild, space is restrictive, and a handful of successes can't justify keeping large numbers of animals.

facts.text: The animal-welfare charity Born Free Foundation argues that most species kept in zoos are not threatened in the wild, very few zoo animals return to the wild, and zoo space remains restrictive.
Born Free argues that citing a handful of zoo-bred species returned to the wild risks implying many more exist, and cannot justify keeping large numbers of mostly unthreatened species.

title: Animals that flew before people
description: Fruit flies went up first, in 1947, and came back alive. Laika became the first living creature to orbit Earth in 1957 and died within hours. Belka and Strelka orbited and came home in 1960, and Ham the chimpanzee flew in January 1961, months before Yuri Gagarin.

facts.text: The first animals intentionally sent into space were fruit flies, launched on a V-2 rocket on 20 February 1947; they came back alive.
On November 3, 1957, the dog Laika, a stray from Moscow's streets, became the first living creature launched into Earth orbit, aboard Sputnik 2.

Sputnik 2 had no way to return, and Laika died of overheating about five to seven hours after launch; Soviet officials said she lived for days, and the truth came out in 2002. A statue honors her in Moscow.
On August 19, 1960, the dogs Belka and Strelka orbited Earth on Sputnik 5 and came home alive.
On January 31, 1961, the chimpanzee Ham flew a suborbital Mercury-Redstone flight to test whether tasks could be done in space, and returned safely.
Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space on April 12, 1961, aboard Vostok 1.

title: Why animals went to space first
description: Nobody knew whether living bodies could survive spaceflight: weightlessness and radiation were unknowns. Fruit flies tested radiation and came back without mutations; Ham tested whether tasks could be done in space.

facts.text: Before human spaceflight, a prevailing worry was that humans might not be able to survive long periods of weightlessness.
The 1947 fruit flies were small, light and easy to store; after recovery, scientists found radiation had not mutated their genetics, which paved the way for human flight.

title: Biomimicry and Velcro
description: Biomimicry imitates natural designs in engineering. Velcro came from burdock burrs (a plant) that stuck to George de Mestral and his dog: tiny hooks, paired with loops, patented in 1955.

facts.text: Biomimicry is the imitation of natural biological designs or processes in engineering or invention.

Near Lausanne, Switzerland, George de Mestral found burrs of the burdock plant stuck to his clothes and his dog's fur; under a microscope they bore tiny hooks, and he patented a hook-and-loop fastener in 1955.
The name Velcro combines the French words velours (velvet) and crochet (hook).

title: Kingfisher trains and gecko grippers
description: The 500 Series Shinkansen's nose copies the kingfisher's beak to end tunnel booms. Gecko toe hairs stick by van der Waals forces, and NASA JPL's gecko-inspired grippers work even in a vacuum.

facts.text: Early Shinkansen trains made a loud tunnel boom leaving tunnels; the nose of JR West's 500 Series, in service from 1997, copies the kingfisher's beak, which lets it dive into water with barely a splash.
The kingfisher-shaped nose ended the tunnel booms and let the train run about 10 percent faster on about 15 percent less electricity.
Geckos are small reptiles whose toe pads are covered with tiny hairlike structures that let them climb smooth, vertical surfaces.
Gecko foot hairs, the smallest hundreds of times thinner than a human hair, stick by van der Waals forces: weak, temporary attractions between atoms.
NASA JPL's gecko-inspired grippers use synthetic hairs that stick when pressed and release when the force is removed; they work in a vacuum and gripped objects in microgravity tests.
